The study examines whether the anticipation of a monthly salary influences consumer decisions and spending patterns, potentially leading to payday-related arbitrage opportunities in Swedish marketplaces. By scrutinizing transaction data from Tradera, this research seeks to reveal if there is a discernible fluctuation in prices that corresponds with the inflow of regular salaries. Our analysis uncovers a modest but statistically significant increase in bidding activity post-payday, with a 2% rise in prices and a notable increase in bid volumes. However, this effect does not translate into substantial arbitrage opportunities due to the platform's fee structure and shipping costs. Intriguingly, day-of-the-week patterns emerged as more influential in shaping bidding behavior than payday effects. These findings contribute to the understanding of consumer market dynamics in response to synchronized salary disbursements, enriching the discourse on behavioral finance and auction theory.

records.title: Private Equity: The Secret  Sauce for Pandemic-Proof  Performance or Just Another  Quarantine Regret? How PE-backed companies performed during COVID-19 pandemic compared to non-PE-backed companies
records.abstract: This study utilizes a dataset comprising 99 private equity-backed firms and 317 non-private equity-backed firms in Sweden to investigate whether private equity-backed firms were more resilient during the COVID-19 pandemic compared to similar firms using difference-in-differences method. Our findings indicate that private equity-backed firms experienced a significant increase in investment, credit, and equity inflows, and exhibited better operational performance when compared to similar firms in the wake of the COVID-19 outbreak. Additionally, our analysis yields mixed results regarding the effect that private equity has on financially constrained firms. Most of the results are consistent with previous studies conducted during the 2008 financial crisis, which suggest that private equity-backed firms are better equipped to navigate financial instability during times of crisis.

records.title: Beyond Credit Ratings: The Role of (E)SG in Sovereign Debt Investments
records.abstract: The study investigates the correlation between ESG performance and sovereign bond yield spreads using regression analysis. The results reveal a significant negative correlation between the Governance and Social indices and bond spreads, emphasising the importance of good governance practices and social stability in reducing the risk of sovereign debt default. However, the Environmental index does not exhibit a significant correlation, possibly due to a time-horizon mismatch and limited selection of environmental variables. Integrating ESG performance, particularly Governance and Social factors, alongside traditional credit ratings can provide investors with a comprehensive view of risk in sovereign debt investments. Monitoring ESG signals and excluding the worst ESG performers from portfolios may help reduce volatility while maintaining portfolio characteristics. The study acknowledges limitations, such as time horizon mismatch, omitted variable bias, and data quality, suggesting avenues for future research to address these limitations and enhance the robustness of the analysis.

records.title: Navigating Uncertainty: A Study on the Impact of Policy Uncertainty on Stock Returns, Firm Investment, and Investor Sentiment in the United States
records.abstract: We investigate how US policy uncertainty is related to US stock returns, firm investments, and investor sentiment - in order to shed light on the responses made by firms and investors when faced with higher uncertainty. Leveraging the economic policy uncertainty index, we find that policy uncertainty is negatively correlated with US stock returns in the same month following a shock to uncertainty, and propose evidence that points towards policy uncertainty potentially being a source of return predictability in the US. Our results also point towards policy uncertainty having effects on the demand for downside protection by looking at how investors respond to shocks in uncertainty, but find no conclusive evidence regarding its effects on market wide investor sentiment. We find a delayed and negative impact on firm investment, implying that policy uncertainty could have an impact on firms' investment decisions as they defer investments in favor of waiting for more information.

records.title: Company Characteristics and Investments Related to ESG Ratings - Does Ownership Have an Impact?
records.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between ownership structure and ESG ranking. Data from companies is used to analyze which types of investors invest in companies with high ESG rankings. The result of the study shows that investment advisors combined with hedge funds invested in companies with high ESG ranking, meanwhile individual investors, separate hedge funds, and separate investment advisors did not invest as much in companies with high ESG ranking. Some strength to ownership as a predictor of increases in ESG rating was present but not conclusive.

records.title: The Patient Risk-Taker: Understanding the Drivers of Wealth and Inequality Across Countries
records.abstract: While economic inequality has been a topic of interest to researchers for decades, most literature is focused on inequality and its evolution in single country analyses, with very little research done on drivers of wealth inequality across countries. This paper documents an association between variations in country-level patience and risk preferences from experiments involving thousands of individuals from 76 countries, and cross-sectional wealth and wealth inequality measures. We find that patience is positively correlated with average wealth. Our results also suggest that patience is associated with a decrease in wealth inequality while risk-taking is associated with an increase in wealth inequality. These associations exist through the wealth distribution and are robust to the empirical specification and a set of controls. We also find that financial development is a driving channel of the observed association between the preferences and wealth.

records.title: Geometric Brownian Motion Option Pricing Model for Professional Football Contracts
records.abstract: In recent years, the valuation of football players has gained significant attention, especially in the context of their transfer value in the market. Our investigation explores the application of a Geometric Brownian Motion option pricing model to estimate the transfer value of football players, considering the option-like characteristics of player contracts. This study is an adaptation to existing models within the football player valuation context, utilizing variables such as player performance, age, contract length, and market conditions. The pricing model is tested on a comprehensive dataset of football players who either transferred between Premier League clubs between 2017-2021 or played 50+ games in the league within the same period. The proposed model is compared to standard valuation methods, such as those based on market comparables or performance metrics. Our preliminary findings indicate that the Geometric Brownian Motion pricing model provides a robust framework for estimating football player transfer values. While our results do not confirm the model's definitive superiority, they highlight its potential in capturing the complex dynamics of football player valuation and provide a foundation for further exploration in this area.

records.title: Beyond Borders: Exploring Investor Sentiment and CCEF Prices
records.abstract: We test the relationship between closed-end country funds (CCEFs) and their relationship with American investors' sentiments toward the respective home country of the funds during the years 2009 to 2021 which were met with adversaries such as COVID-19. Previous research regarding closed-end country funds was done in the 1990s and in the early 2000s, where the research discovered a positive relationship between CCEF price premiums and positive perception of a country. As we considered these studies to not reflect the present-day society that has seen drastic social, economic, and technological changes, we have tested this relationship with a more recent time period. In contrast to existing literature, we find that CCEFs from countries with higher country popularity among American investors are generally traded at a discount.

records.title: Green Minus Brown: A Comparative Analysis of the Financial Performance of the ESG Factor
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the performance of a Green-minus-Brown portfolio in the US public stock market and whether the GMB portfolio provides significant results for investors. The study also aims to investigate if the returns of the GMB portfolio are already explained by other existing factors. The research collected data from 2003 to 2022. Moreover, our findings indicate that there is no significant effect of the GMB portfolio over a longer period of time. Nevertheless, during economic expansions, there are effects in the GMB portfolio that are not explained by existing factors. The findings of the research point at the fact that ESG might not be an ideal and unique factor for investors looking to predict their returns. In light of these results found for the GMB factor, it is fundamental to note that further research in this area is fundamental to better understand the role of the GMB portfolio, especially over longer periods of time and different economic scenarios and markets.

records.title: The Drivers of Wealth Inequality: The Case of Sweden
records.abstract: Wealth inequality is a defining feature of the global economy which gives rise to several societal issues. To investigate the driving factors behind wealth inequality in Sweden, a wealth model from Gabaix et al. (2016) is extended to include type dependency, differences in returns amongst individuals in the population. We construct this model to be calibrated with unique data on household market risk and idiosyncratic risk from Calvet et al. (2007). We accurately represent the distribution of Swedish wealth and use this model to consider insightful counterfactual scenarios. This model shows that idiosyncratic risk and return heterogeneity are strong drivers of wealth inequality. Additionally, we find that increased market participation and better investment strategies for low-wealth households have a limited impact on wealth inequality. Lastly, we find that adjustments to capital gains tax can strongly impact wealth inequality.

records.title: Industry Effects on Stock Price Crash Risk: Quantifying Industry Effects and the Effect of Structural Industry Characteristics
records.abstract: This paper empirically investigates the determinants of stock price crash risk at the industry level. Prior research has largely focused on firm-level and macro-level factors that impact stock price crash risk, with little attention being drawn to inter-industry differences. Using a large sample of US firms from different industries, this paper finds significant industry fixed effects on stock price crash risk, with varying magnitudes between industries. For example, industries in the health care sector are consistently associated with high crash risk, while industries in the energy sector are consistently associated with low crash risk. Furthermore, this study examines possible underlying dynamics of these industry effects by analyzing the effects of three structural industry characteristics on crash risk. The findings indicate a significant positive effect of industry growth rate on stock price crash risk, as well as a significant negative effect of industry profitability during the period 1985-2000. No effects are found for industry concentration, although it is concluded that this may be due to limitations in the proxy used.

records.title: A family affair: The relationship between family control and performance in Swedish public firms
records.abstract: This study examines the influence of family control on market and operational performance among the largest listed companies on Nasdaq Stockholm. Our results reveal that family control has a positive effect on market performance, but not on operational performance. We also find that unaffiliated block holders positively contribute to family firms' operational performance, while family management does not impact firm performance. Contrary to agency theory, family firms with higher agency problems do not exhibit worse performance compared to those with lower agency problems. However, our study finds that the positive impact of family control on market performance is offset when families employ dual share class systems, and their vote holding exceeds their share ownership by more than 25 percentage points.

records.title: Uncorking Profits: Fine Wine for the Bottom Line
records.abstract: Using a larger dataset covering a time period not previously studied, we examine the price drivers and investment performance of wines from the five Bordeaux Premier Cru producers during 2013-2023. Our results indicate that prices are significantly impacted by producer, weather quality, yield and age. We then construct a price index of all wines in our sample using a repeat-sales regression and compare its development to that of other commodities and traditional investments. The results show that investments in fine wine have not been a good endeavour financially over our sample period. However, the results are different between wines of different qualities.

records.title: Changing Patterns over the FOMC Cycle
records.abstract: We document that in the period 2017 to 2022, the US stock market did not feature the same pattern of higher excess stock returns in even weeks following Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announcements as in the period 1994 to 2016. We show that timing of Board of Governors meetings and direction of Fed funds target rate movements affect US market returns in both periods, and connect changes in these factors to the distortion of the even-week return pattern. The behavior of uncertainty over the FOMC cycle, both for the 1994-2016 and the 2017- 2022 period, shows that drops in uncertainty neither are unique to the time of FOMC announcements nor persist in the post-sample period. Followingly, we argue that the resolution of a FOMC uncertainty risk premium is not what drives return- patterns around FOMC announcements.

records.title: Sustainable Investments in Times of Crisis
records.abstract: This paper examines the effect of Covid-19 on green and brown funds in the Swedish Premium Pension System (PPS). We apply the methodology derived in Berk and van Binsbergen (2015) in a difference-in-difference model with time-fixed effects to estimate the average effect of Covid-19 on green funds for both value added and conventional alpha measures. We find that, prior to the pandemic, green funds managed more money relative to brown funds, but green fund managers were compensated less compared to their conventional counterparts because of lower fees. After the pandemic, the relative difference in assets under management grew, and managerial compensation for green funds increased accordingly. Our results, obtained using three benchmarking methods to calculate abnormal return, suggest a relative decrease in gross alpha for green funds after the outbreak of Covid-19, primarily due to substantial inflows of capital. However, the effect on gross alpha is not statistically significant. We document a relative increase in value added for green funds during the pandemic, which is primarily attributable to larger cross-sectional differences in assets under management. Our findings contribute to a diverse body of literature on sustainable investments in crisis and provide Swedish pension savers with novel insights.

records.title: Did Private Equity-Backed Firms Outperform Operationally During Covid-19?
records.abstract: Do private equity (PE) backed companies perform better operationally in a non-financial crisis? By analyzing PE-backed firms in the UK during Covid-19 using fixed effects difference-in-differences, our findings suggest that private equity-backed companies' performance decreased significantly more at the onset of the crisis and increased their leverage but recovered faster both with greater magnitude and significance. PE-backed companies thus seem to handle an operationally-sided crisis better over time but are more exposed to them initially. In conclusion, private equity adds value operationally, but it is not without tradeoffs in terms of risk.

records.title: The Effect of Increasing House Prices on Household Debt in Sweden
records.abstract: By using data on house prices and household debt during the years 2010-2016 the paper aims to determine the effect of increasing house prices on housing debt and debt-to- income across Swedish municipalities. Via an IV approach we find a significant causal relationship between house prices and household debt. Dividing the populations based on net income and population size respectively, indicate that municipality characteristics dictate the relationship between rising house prices and borrowing behavior among households, and that the magnitude of the effect varies significantly within the country. We find a stronger tendency to increase debt to income ratio among households in both lower income municipalities and in municipalities with less population.

records.title: Exploring the Diversification Benefits  of NFT Sectors
records.abstract: This study investigates the evolving diversification benefits of adding Non-Fungible Token (NFT) sector indices to a portfolio consisting of traditional assets. Focusing on two investor types with contrasting risk appetites, this research examines the diversification potential before and after the 2020 Bullrun. Contrary to prior findings, results indicate that the diversification benefits of NFTs have increased over time, benefiting investors across the risk spectrum. Additionally, the study highlights the varying diversification potential of different NFT sectors. The findings challenge the notion that NFTs' diversification advantages have diminished, revealing the importance of considering NFTs as a diverse market rather than a singular asset type. This study paves the way for further investigation into the drivers of diversification benefits in different market conditions and NFT subcategories.

records.title: The Insider Scoop: A Study on the Effect of Insider Trading and Abnormal Stock Returns During Uncertain Market Condition of the Russia-Ukraine War
records.abstract: This paper examines how insider transactions of stocks listed on Nasdaq Stockholm generate abnormal returns during the period 2016-2022 and extends on how abnormal returns react in times of uncertainty, i.e., after the Invasion of Ukraine. Our findings suggest that there are smaller abnormal returns connected with insider trading in the timeframe of 2016-2022, but not necessarily as highly connected in times of uncertainty. This paper confirms the foundation set by previous studies, even though the stock market has gone through a shift of paradigm. Ultimately this thesis opens for more in-depth future research revolving around the new environment of the capital market along with insider trading and the behavioural phenomenon around it.

records.title: The Impact of Carbon Emissions on Stock Returns
records.abstract: We investigate the carbon emissions' effect on stock returns in European firms. The results show that firms with higher carbon intensity, a relative measure of carbon emission, yield a higher stock return while controlling for return-predicting factors. This suggests the existence of a carbon premium to compensate investors for additional carbon-related risk. We also note that for total emissions and emissions growth as independent variables, there are no statistically significant effects supporting the carbon risk premium hypothesis. Overall, we find weaker evidence for the existence of a carbon premium than previous, mainly American, research on the topic.

records.title: Weathering the Storm: A Difference-in-Differences Study on Nordic Private Equity Performance and M&A Activity During the Covid-19 Pandemic
records.abstract: Using financial data for Nordic private equity-backed companies, this paper investigates the performance and M&A activity of private equity-owned firms during the covid-19 pandemic. The results show that sales, investments and the number of add-on acquisitions increased significantly for private equity-owned firms compared to their peers in 2020 and 2021. Robustness tests confirm the results for investments and the number of add-on acquisitions, but not for sales. Additionally, investments and private equity ownership increased the likelihood of purchasing an add-on acquisition during the covid-19 pandemic. This paper provides insight into how private equity-backed firms perform in times of crisis and whether private equity ownership contributes to financial stability. This study's findings have implications for PE investors since the results shed light on the importance of agility and flexibility in responding to unpredictable events and market conditions.

records.title: Unemployment and Household Debt - A Practical Example
records.abstract: In the previous literature, a theoretical correlation has been established in between household indebtedness and the unemployment rate. This study uses several forms of regressions and OECD data on the years 1995 - 2021 to see if this correlation exists in practice. After accounting for fixed effects, the correlation is deemed to be positive, thus reinforcing the previous literature. Further research is needed to find causal factors, possible reasons for which can be consumption reduction due to high debt obligations, decreased investment in human capital and diminished workers' bargaining power.

records.title: Green Goes Green: To What Extent Does A Company's ESG Rating Correlate With Its Stock Performance During The Covid-19 Pandemic? A Panel Data Regression Study On The EU Stock Market
records.abstract: This thesis examines the relationship between ESG scores and financial performance during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, using a sample of over 1,000 stocks from the EU and Schengen countries. For the overall market, the results revealed no significant relationship between the pre-2020 ESG score and financial performance. However, social and environmental scores had a positive relationship while governance had a negative relationship. Looking at specific sectors, the results varied between and within sectors. Some sectors, such as the IT and consumer discretionary sectors, had positive relationships with their respective pre-2020 ESG- scores. In contrast, other sectors had a negative relationship, such as the financial sector. Furthermore, the results display a number of insignificant relationships suggesting that investing in ESG activities may not have had an impact on financial performance during spring 2020.

records.title: Is Everyone Uninformed? A study of the relationship between profitability and IPO underpricing
records.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the explanatory power of profitability on IPO underpricing through the lens of information asymmetry over different time paradigms. We find that although profitability does not have an impact on IPO underpricing in general, during the time paradigm of 2001 to 2010 it has a positive significant impact- highlighting the necessity to account for variations over time. This result is contrary to traditional information asymmetry theories and goes against past research findings. We propose to understand this result partly through the variation of informational value of accounting fundamentals in equity valuations over time and a potential mediating effect of news and marketing efforts by investment banks on uninformed investors' post-offering trading behaviour. We hypothesise that during the post-Dot-com bubble paradigm, investment banks were cautious to market firms with questionable financial track records. We propose future researchers to empirically investigate this hypothesis as an explanation of our results.

records.title: Broken promises: The failure of green stock outperformance in Europe - the importance of rating coherence
records.abstract: Increasing interest for sustainable investment have caused a trend within the investment sector towards more ESG engagements. Our study finds no outperformance of green portfolios over brown portfolios, when using industry-adjusted environmental pillar scores. The same applies when controlling for unexpected climate concerns. However, we do find evidence of across-industry greenness having more impact on stock returns when including both measures of greenness. This indicates that within-industry alone does not have the capacity to capture stock return variations to explain any green outperformance. Lastly, we provide evidence that the choice of model in calculating unexpected climate concerns significantly impacts the interaction between greenness and unexpected climate concerns.

records.title: The Spillover Effects of Intrastate Conflicts on FDI Flows in Countries Neighbouring the Conflict
records.abstract: The purpose of this study is to investigate the spillover effect of intrastate wars on neighbouring nations net FDI inflows by categorising battle deaths into different thresholds and regressing FDI on those thresholds. The research design is based on a two-way fixed effects model with country and time fixed effects. The sample period is from 1970-2019 and the sample consists of all countries in the World. We aim to fill the gap in the literature between FDI and conflict spillovers, by providing insight into their intersection. We find that battle deaths in neighbouring countries, on average, have positive and significant effects on FDI inflows for a given country.

records.title: In the Line of Fire: A Study of Market Efficiency in the Context of Wildfires and Stock Market Reactions
records.abstract: Climate research finds that climate change and raising global temperatures increase the risk and severity of wildfires. However, the impact varies substantially based on geographical location and causes a dispersion in wildfire trends. Utilizing data from 14 countries, we investigate if wildfire severity trends have a material impact on the profitability of the forestry and paper & pulp (P&P) industries and whether the stock market is efficiently pricing these trends. We find that a poor wildfire trend ranking for a country forecasts lower profitability growth and that the market responds efficiently in terms of correctly pricing this climate change-related risk.
records.lds04: Bachelor Thesis in Accounting and Financial Management

records.title: ESG Ratings and Stock Market Performance: Evidence of a Shift in Investor Preferences during a Period of Economic Distress in Scandinavia
records.abstract: During the Covid-19 crisis, firms with high environmental, social, and governance (ESG) ratings traded within the Scandinavian markets had more significant pandemic-induced drops in stock returns than firms with low profiles in ESG. The difference was close to ten percentage points more severe for high-ESG compared to low-ESG firms. This evidence suggests that in a region with fundamentally high levels of ESG engagement, investors tend to ward off high-ESG firms when faced with a downturn in the real economy. We hence emphasize the need to recognize the unique effects of regions that deviate from a global trend and to extend the focus beyond financial capital when attempting to understand the determinants of firm-level performance during a crisis.

records.title: The Carbon Conundrum: Investigating the Relationship Between Carbon Risk and Eurozone Corporate Bond Returns
records.abstract: We examine whether carbon risk, proxied by a firm's carbon emission intensity (CEI), is priced in the cross-section of the Eurozone corporate bond market. Using rolling regressions to estimate systematic risk factor loadings and then conducting panel regressions under different fixed effects combinations, we examine the varying dynamics that affect the pricing of carbon risk in the bond market. We find that bonds issued by firms with higher CEI systematically earn lower returns, indicating a mispricing at a broader level, although the economic effect is marginal at -0.1 basis points. Further investigation suggests that the pricing of carbon risk is episodic in nature and context-sensitive rather than being consistently integrated overtime in the bond market. Disruptive periods such as COVID-19 amplify the mispricing due to intensified climate concerns and shifts in investor preferences leading to lower returns for bonds of high-CEI firms relative to others. Outside such disruptions, carbon risk is priced significantly within industries. In the stable and longer run, carbon risk is priced at a more localized level, reflecting the influence of changing sectoral norms in favor of sustainability and investors' attention to their local contexts.

records.title: The Price of Going Public: Examining IPO Underpricing and Information Asymmetry During the COVID-19 Hot Issue Market
records.abstract: We examine the spike in IPO underpricing during COVID-19 from the perspective of traditional theories of adverse selection, which suggest that underpricing follows from uncertainty about the quality of firms going public. Using a sample of 1,026 U.S. IPOs from 2017 to 2022, we find little evidence of increased dispersion in firm quality during the pandemic. We also analyze certification mechanisms, such as underwriter reputation, and find that while it reduces underpricing, its effect does not intensify during the pandemic. Instead, significant underperformance in longer-term returns for IPOs issued during the pandemic suggests alternative explanations, such as investor sentiment, motivating future research to explore behavioral drivers of the pandemic IPO market.

records.title: An Investigation of Diseconomies of Scale in Volatile Markets under short-term Periods: Analyzing the Impact of fund-specific Variables on Mutual Fund Performance during Market Turbulence
records.abstract: This thesis explores the relationship between mutual fund size and performance during market volatility, focusing on U.S.-equity actively managed mutual funds from 2019 to 2023. Unlike findings from stable, long-term periods, no significant relationship is observed between assets under management and benchmark-adjusted returns in this turbulent time frame. Turnover ratio emerges as a key factor, showing a significant negative relationship with gross and net returns, likely due to higher trading costs, and a weak negative relationship with fund size, suggesting larger funds trade less actively. However, low R² values indicate limited explanatory power. These results highlight the complexity of fund performance during volatile periods and the need for broader research to better understand the interplay between fund-specific and market-level factors.

records.title: The Impact of Going Public on the Firm Scale and Commercialisation Strategy
records.abstract: We examine the impact of Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) on firm scale and commercialisation strategy on Swedish firms that went public between 2001 and 2020. We construct a matched control group of private firms and employ a difference-in-difference methodology to analyse how changes in total assets, net sales, employees, sales per employee, profitability, workplaces, subsidiaries, and geographical presence differ between IPO firms and their matched private counterparts. We find that IPOs drive significant growth in total assets, net sales, employees, and workplaces, and that firms expand into new cities and countries. However, we observe no significant improvements in profitability, productivity, or the number of subsidiaries post-IPO. Our results highlight the role of IPOs in shifting towards a strategy of increased commercialisation and international operational expansion.

records.title: Quantifying Sources of Firm-Level Risk Through Conference Call Transcripts: A BERTopic Approach
records.abstract: We use BERTopic to develop an alternative approach to measuring topic-specific risk for firms from quarterly earnings conference calls. This approach allows us to both discover and quantify sources of firm risk based on statements made by company executives. We show the topics identified by the model are coherent and that the aggregate risk patterns for each are intuitive based on historical context. Seven out of the thirteen risks we study are significant and positively correlated with future realised stock volatility. After controlling for firm fixed effects, only two remain significant, suggesting that our measure may primarily reflect permanent differences in firm risk. We decompose the variance structure of each risk and find that global economy, inflation, and supply chain risk are the most systematic. We also find that for cybersecurity, firms exhibit heterogeneous exposure to the aggregate risk along with large and persistent differences in firm-specific risk levels.

records.title: Tracking the Passive Pulse: Unraveling ETFs'    Role in Corporate Investment
records.abstract: This study examines the relationship between ETF ownership and corporate investment sensitivity to stock price signals, focusing on firm size as a moderating factor. Using data from 2005-2015 and employing two instrumental variable (IV) approaches to address endogeneity, we analyze small-, mid-, and large-cap firms, while distinguishing between market and non-market ETFs. The findings suggest that while mid-cap firms exhibit a modest increase in investment sensitivity driven by ETF ownership, the effect diminishes for small-cap and large-cap firms, where interaction terms remain consistently insignificant. These results challenge prior assumptions about ETFs amplifying price informativeness, particularly when firm size is accounted for. By introducing size-based disaggregation, this study underscores the nuanced and potentially limited role of ETFs in shaping corporate investment.

records.title: ETF Flows: a Lens for Predicting Market Returns
records.abstract: This study examines the return predictability of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) across the U.S., European, and Asia-Pacific markets, based on primary market fund flows, using both static and dynamic portfolio strategies. We show that the arbitrage activities of Authorized Participants (creation and redemption of ETF shares) signal non-fundamental demand shocks and predict subsequent ETF price and NAV returns. In the U.S., static portfolio analysis reveals significant variations among ETF returns in terms of fund flow patterns, where ETFs with high share redemption outperform those with high share creation. At the same time, Europe exhibits weaker return predictability, which can be reflected by higher arbitrage barriers and lower market liquidity. The Asia-Pacific market shows weaker short-term predictability and stronger long-term effects, indicating more effective price correction mechanisms compared to Europe but less efficiency than the U.S. We also show that ETF price reversal mechanisms in the short-term can be used in hedging trading strategies between ETFs and their underlying asset baskets.

records.title: Short-Termism in Swedish Corporate Investments: A Comparison of Publicly Listed and Private Firms. A Historical and Comparative Perspective.
records.abstract: This study examines Swedish firms' investment behaviors during the period 2001-2011. We examine the investment behaviors of stock market listed firms and private firms in Sweden to evaluate the impact of short-termism pressures on corporate decision-making. Using robust matching procedures, we treat private firms that are similar to publicly listed firms as a counterfactual to model how publicly listed firms might behave in the absence of short-term market pressures. Our results suggest that publicly listed firms do not exhibit lower investment levels or sensitivities compared to private firms. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to several methodological limitations, including challenges related to the matching procedure and potential selection bias, as well as the absence of randomized experimental settings. While these results contribute to the discourse on corporate governance and short-termism, they underscore the need for further research to isolate the effects of market pressures more conclusively.

records.title: Truckloads of Power: Unpacking Market Concentration in U.S. Trucking
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the implications of increasing market concentration in the U.S. trucking industry, focusing on the profitability drivers asset utilization and market power during the 2001-2014 period. Drawing on comprehensive regression analyses and a deep-dive industry approach, the study examines whether profitability gains stem from efficiency improvements or firms leveraging market power. Findings reveal a significant positive relationship between concentration and profitability, driven primarily by increased profit margins as captured by the Lerner Index, rather than operational efficiencies measured by asset utilization. Contrary to initial hypotheses, the trucking industry's profitability aligns with aggregate market trends, where market power appears to dominate over efficiency gains as the source of abnormal profits. However, the results show a decreased magnitude of the profit margin effect. This is speculated to be attributed to the minimization of efficiency gains captured by the Lerner index prominent in other industries. This study contributes to the broader debate on market consolidation's economic impact and provides insights for policymakers and corporate managers on navigating the balance between efficiency and market power in a concentrated market landscape.

records.title: A comparative study of venture capital influence on IPO performance in the US
records.abstract: In this paper, we compare the performance of venture capital-backed IPOs with the performance of non-venture capital-backed IPOs in the US from 1980 to 2020 using a variety of performance metrics such as Underpricing, Buy and Hold Abnormal Returns (BHAR), Property, Plant, and Equipment (PPE) as a measure of Investments, Return on Assets (ROA) and Sales Growth. We provide evidence that VC-backed IPOs portray strong long-term performance owing to high growth ambitions and strategic investments but often compromise profitability. One of the key focus areas of our study is the 2008 financial crisis. We find that during the crisis, VC-backed IPOs showed more resilience compared to their non-VC-backed counterparts. By controlling for industry and year-fixed effects, this study aims to provide evidence for the value-added and the dynamic role played by venture capitals in helping firms achieve strong IPO performance.

records.title: Private Equity's Appetite for Engineering: Investigating the performance effects of private equity ownership during exogenous shocks
records.abstract: This paper examines the performance of European small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) backed by private equity (PE) firms compared to non-PE-backed counterparts during two consecutive, unrelated crises: the COVID-19 pandemic and the Ukraine war. Our findings reveal that PE-backed SMEs underperform in terms of profitability, although this divergence only occurs in 2022. We further analyze two key value drivers of PE portfolio companies' profitability: operational engineering and financial engineering. Over the course of the crises, PE-backed SMEs face challenges stemming from initial heavy financial engineering at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and exhibit signs of reduced operational efficiency. Combined, what should have created value for the companies, leads to reduced profitability short-term.

records.title: Sharper Strategies: Global Patterns & Local Precision in Stock Return Prediction Through Transfer Learning with Convolutional Neural Networks
records.abstract: This paper explores the potential of transfer learning with convolutional neural networks to improve stock return predictions. The transfer learning models are compared to models trained on local market data as well as the direct application of models trained on U.S. data. Analyzing daily data of individual stocks, across 22 countries from 1993 to 2024, the study evaluates two transfer learning models: one that fine-tunes decision-making layers while retaining pre-trained patterns and another that fully adapts all layers to local data. The findings reveal that leveraging a model pre-trained on U.S. data generally enhances performance, particularly when the local dataset is below a certain size. However, the impact of retraining on local data is mixed, with results varying significantly across different markets.

records.title: Sustainable Investing in the Nordics: What is most important - Environmental, Social or Governance Scores?
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the relationship between ESG scores and financial performance in the Nordic region from 2013 to 2022, utilizing a sample of over 400 stocks. It also explores which aspect of ESG - Environmental, Social, or Governance - has the greatest influence on financial performance. The findings indicate that stocks with higher ESG scores outperformed those with lower scores during the study period. Additionally, the results suggest that the social and governance components of ESG significantly impact financial performance, with the social aspect having the strongest effect. However, while the environmental component has a significant impact when considered in isolation, its influence became insignificant when assessed alongside the other ESG factors.

records.title: Diversity Dividens: Gender Dynamics and Corporate Performance in Sweden. A Financial Perspective on Gender Diversity in Swedish Boardrooms
records.abstract: This study examines the impact of gender diversity on corporate boards on firm financial performance within the Swedish stock market. Using performance-based measures like Tobin's Q and accounting measures such as ROA and ROE, the study employs multiple regression analysis on panel data from 2014 to 2022. It evaluates the influence of female board members while controlling for factors like firm size, leverage, average age, and board size. The analysis is underpinned by several corporate governance theories-Agency Theory, Stakeholder Theory, and Resource Dependency Theory-and theories addressing behavioral differences between genders, specifically Risk Aversion Theory and Legitimacy Theory. Based on the methodology of Ahren & Dittmar (2012), this study expands the analysis to include both market and accounting metrics. Results indicate no significant impact of gender diversity on Tobin's Q, ROA, and ROE, highlighting the complex nature of this relationship. The broader societal and ethical implications of gender diversity are emphasized, suggesting the need for further investigation.

records.title: Sports Betting as an Alternative Investment
records.abstract: This paper provides a broad overview of sports betting, considering its markets and evaluating whether it can provide positive risk-adjusted returns as an alternative financial investment. Across a large dataset of closing odds from over 165,000 soccer games from top European leagues, we develop a trading strategy which generates promising returns. We then conduct a survey of sports-betting models in academic literature, obtaining a representative distribution of returns from betting across sports, combining this with detailed data for prices and events to simulate a fictional sports-betting asset. With a returns profile for this asset, we then include it in an optimised mean-variance portfolio, integrating it with conventional asset indices, finding that the sports-betting asset compares favourably in various investing scenarios, including a value-at-risk analysis. Finally, we discuss financial frictions specific to this market, concluding that sports betting does not provide sufficient liquidity for large wealth managers, but that shrewd investors with a nuanced understanding of the market can likely generate strong returns.

records.title: The Impact of Scale in Active Fund Management: Examining Diseconomies of Scale in Actively Managed Mutual Funds Investing in European Equities
records.abstract: We empirically investigate the relationship between fund size and performance using a comprehensive sample of actively managed mutual funds investing in European equities. We find statistically significant evidence of decreasing returns to scale in active fund management. As the size of a fund increases, its ability to outperform its corresponding benchmark declines. In addition, we find a statistically significant negative relationship between fund age and benchmark-adjusted performance. Furthermore, we find that both the average benchmark-adjusted gross return and the value-added measure are positive for the funds in our sample, implying that fund managers can generate excess returns. However, these returns are diminished for investors due to fees, resulting in investor returns averaging below those of the funds' benchmarks. Finally, we find that the expense ratio of a fund is an important determinant of the fund's benchmark-adjusted net return, thus challenging the neoclassical model of mutual funds, where fees are deemed negligible as an investment criterion.

records.title: Outperforming S&P 500: The power of using earnings quality in fundamental stock selection
records.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the relationship between quality of earnings and stock returns, by measuring whether higher (lower) earnings quality corresponds with a higher (lower) stock return, focusing specifically on the constituents of S&P 500. To assess the potential of each individual stock, we construct a Quality-of-Earnings (QoE) Score composed of five variables. Through portfolio regressions based on 20 years of historical data, this non-experimental, observational study finds abnormal returns ranging between 4.3-5.2% annually depending on the update frequency (annual, three-year, or five-year) of the QoE Score portfolios. We also find that one of the variables itself, the Margin Score portfolio, finds alpha of 12.6-14.6% annually, depending on the update frequency. Finally, we conclude that all QoE Score portfolios, regardless of the update frequency, outperform the S&P 500 in terms of both absolute and risk-adjusted returns.

records.title: Do IPOs Affect Prices of Other Assets? Evidence From a Swedish Setting
records.abstract: This paper looks at effect of IPOs on both market and industry returns through using a sample of 149 IPOs between 2005-2022. We find evidence that sizeable IPOs depress market returns during the pre-offering period where the impact is negatively correlated with size. Through looking at the covariance between IPOs and industries we find that IPOs permanently decreases industry returns on the listing day where the covariance and the return have an inverse relationship. This depressive effect is amplified when we look at the impact of large IPOs as they have an additional depressive effect on industry returns during the pre-offering period, offering date and listing period. We find support for a portfolio rebalancing hypothesis where industry prices depress due to a substitution effect.

records.title: Replicating Success: Adopting the Value-Added Method to Assess Managerial Skill in Luxembourg and the rest of Europe
records.abstract: This study examines the managerial skill for Luxembourg's equity mutual fund market by using Berk and van Binsbergen's (2015) value-added method and using the rest of Europe as a comparison. In contrast to prior literature the results show that the managers in Luxembourg and the rest of Europe fail to persistently add value and to some extent even destroy it. Additionally, when investigating the investors' ability to predict skill, through managerial compensation, the results indicate that they are incapable of predicting performance. These results refute our hypothesis that Luxembourg fund managers could leverage from the benefit of a financial hub. Thus, the study concludes the inexistence of managerial skill in Luxembourg and the rest of Europe.

records.title: Investing in trust: Examining the impact of CSR on stock returns during market crisis
records.abstract: This paper examines the impact of social capital, as measured by corporate social responsibility (CSR), on stock returns during economic downturns, specifically the Covid-19 crash and the 2022 market downturn. It highlights the nuanced role of CSR during different types of economic stress and adds a contemporary dimension to existing literature by offering a new perspective on investor behavior in the context of recent global challenges. I find that higher CSR intensity had a positive and significant impact on stock returns during the 2022 market downturn, albeit influenced by the firm's broader financial health. However, this relationship was not evident during the Covid-19 crash, suggesting that the nature of the economic downturn could be pivotal in CSR's protective value.

records.title: Riding the Wave: IPO Underpricing on the London Stock Exchange between 2008 and 2023
records.abstract: Initial Public Offering (IPO) underpricing has been observed on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) since 1917. Between 2008 and 2023, an IPO underpricing of 13.21% was found, disrupting the previous increasing pattern between 1917 and 2007. This decrease in IPO underpricing can be attributed to enhanced regulatory frameworks, which increased trust and reduced information asymmetry. Of the previously statistically significant factors impacting IPO underpricing on the LSE, only market capitalisation remains significant. The negative estimate of this factor indicates that larger firms still experience less IPO underpricing. Moreover, no trends in IPO underpricing are identified when comparing the pre- and post-Brexit periods, signifying Brexit's limited effect on IPO underpricing.

records.title: The Effect of Insider Transactions on Stock Prices
records.abstract: The paper examines how FSA announcements regarding insider transactions affect stock prices and if abnormal returns can be earned from mimicking the transactions of insiders. 50 stocks from the Swedish market are used as a sample and only acquisitions and disposals of shares are investigated. Two sub-samples are analyzed, the first one being how the magnitude of the transaction affects stock prices and the second one being how different managerial positions have different effects on stock prices. An event study is conducted to investigate any abnormal returns. The results show that the semi-strong and strong form of the efficient market hypothesis does not hold and that abnormal returns can be earned.

records.title: Playing The Numbers Game: Examining Strategic Rounding of EPS Data in Sweden
records.abstract: This thesis explores strategic rounding in earnings per share (EPS) in Sweden from 2003 to 2023 by analyzing the frequency of the third decimal digit in EPS data, with an in-depth focus on the digit 4. Contrary to previous US data research, we find no proof that a rounding bias exists in the third decimal place. We test our findings over time, by firms, and for firm factors, being size, EPS magnitude, and growth-value dynamics, where none show signs that rounding occurs. We consider whether currency affects rounding incentives by applying a comparative approach with other Nordic countries but fail to find support. Examining the second decimal place indicates that rounding might occur as zeroes are overrepresented and nines are underrepresented, which could be analyzed further in future research. Our findings contribute to the research field by showcasing different results in another geographical market compared to previous literature, as well as examining the potential effect currencies have on rounding incentives.

records.title: Unexpected National Football Results' Influence on National Stock Markets: Differences in Integrated and Non-Integrated Markets
records.abstract: Using an event study approach with panel data, this paper investigates the abnormal stock market returns of national indices following an unexpected international football result. We utilise football results as a mood proxy, to better examine the effects of cognitive biases and emotional biases on the stock market. We report a negative abnormal return of -67.9 basis points following a draw for countries with low stock market integration and high football popularity. For the difference between the win abnormal return and the loss abnormal return, we report a significant positive value of 30.1 basis points for countries with low stock market integration. Finally, we also document these results by accounting for stock market noise where we find an abnormal stock return the day after a win of 29.4 basis points for countries with low stock market integration.

records.title: ETF Arbitrage, Executed by the Hidden Market Player
records.abstract: By investigating how non-fundamental demand shocks in the primary market affect ETF returns in the US, we find that there exists an explanatory power with a positive return direction. Specifically, by having Authorized Participants that create and redeem ETF shares to correct the law of one price, called ETF Flow, we show that the flow explains the ETF- and their underlying assets' subsequent returns. Moreover, we study how fast these non-fundamental returns can recover back to their fundamental value by splitting our sample into four subsamples to get a better sense of the relationship between the recovery rate and the ETF characteristics. Consequently, the price reversal effect and excess volatility work as the main explanations for the recovery phenomena.

records.title: Inventory Effects: Market Makers' Impact on Short-term Returns
records.abstract: According to the inventory paradigm, market makers are not risk-neutral and demand risk premiums for holding positions. An order book imbalance can lead to inventory build-up of market makers. Price pressures caused by market makers' unloading of positions following build-up of inventory can potentially affect prices and, in extension, returns. This paper investigates whether stock trading strategies that trade in the direction of the previous day's order imbalances are profitable and the relationship between the order imbalance one day and the returns of the next day, using linear regressions. Even if it is not profitable to trade directly on lagged order imbalances, it should be of interest to anyone trading the markets if there exists a relationship between lagged order imbalances and returns. We cannot prove a relationship between one day's order imbalance and the following day's return, and the tested trading strategies do not produce statistically significant returns.

records.title: Unveiling the pilars of M&A performance in US. pharma: a quantitative study on short-term shareholder value in the pharmaceutical indutry
records.abstract: This paper examines the performance of mergers and acquisitions (M&As) within the US pharmaceutical industry during the period of 2019 to 2023. Through an analysis of cumulative abnormal returns in an event study, measuring financial ratios pre- and post merger and their correlation in a multiple linear regression we aim to answer our research question. An inverse relation between profit margin and the cumulative abnormal return was discovered, which showed statistical significance. However, looking at the overall results and financial stability we found no evidence of significant gains associated with a merger. Consequently, rejecting the hypothesis that mergers and acquisitions generate short-term value for shareholders. Thus this paper raises the possibility of alternative reasons as to why mergers and acquisitions take place and remain a strategy of interest.

records.title: Pay to Win? The Effect of Commissioned Equity Research on Stock Prices
records.abstract: This thesis examines the impact of coverage initiation reports by commissioned equity research analysts on stock prices, with a unique focus on Swedish small- and mid-cap stocks. The sample encompasses companies receiving coverage from six different financial institutions between 2014 and 2024. A comprehensive event study using the market model is conducted on the sample containing stocks that have initiated coverage with a first financial institution to find average and cumulative average abnormal returns. A significant increase in the average abnormal returns on the day the report is published demonstrates that initiating coverage leads to a short-term positive shock on the stock prices. Further analysis is conducted by comparing subsamples, such as companies that had coverage terminated compared to companies that are still receiving coverage, companies initiating coverage with specialized research firms compared to companies initiating coverage with larger banks, and companies initiating coverage with their first financial institution compared to companies initiating coverage with a second financial institution. Significant average abnormal returns on the initiation day are found for all subsamples except the sample containing companies initiating coverage with a second financial institution.

records.title: International Bank Flow Dynamics after the Global Financial Crisis: Measuring the Impact of Bank Regulation and Institutional Quality on Foreign Claims Growth
records.abstract: This paper examines the role of country-level bank regulatory reforms, and institutional quality in shaping cross-border capital flows following the Global Financial Crisis. Our study reveals that there has been a clear shift in the determinants of bank inflows from advanced to emerging market economies. Post-crisis findings suggest a diminished impact of institutional quality variables on the annual growth of foreign claims. Additionally, contrary to our pre-crisis results, more stringent bank regulatory regimes deterred foreign investment flows, underscoring the changing dynamics of global capital movements. Hence, our research contributes to understanding the evolving relationship between banking regulations, institutional quality, and international capital flows after the Global Financial Crisis.

records.title: It's Raining Yen: A Study on the Household Response to the Japanese Special Cash Payments
records.abstract: This study analyses the savings, investment, and debt repayment responses of Japanese households to the Special Cash Payments (SCP) distributed as part of the government's COVID-19 economic relief measures in 2020. While previous Japanese studies have focused on the marginal propensity to consume out of the SCP, this paper provides novel insights into households' broader financial decisions following an unanticipated positive income shock. Using monthly panel data from the Family Income and Expenditure Survey across 52 cities in Japan, I employ an instrumental variable approach to estimate the proportion of the SCP used for saving, investment, and debt repayment. I find that on average, households demonstrated a strong propensity to save the SCP funds, a reduced propensity for debt repayment in response to the SCP and an insignificant investment response. In contrast, households with liquidity constraints showed an increased propensity to save, invest and repay debt compared to unconstrained households, suggesting heterogeneous effects based on liquidity constraints.

records.title: Are Sinners Winners? A Study on Sin Stock Performance Between 2020-2023
records.abstract: This paper examines the performance of sin stocks listed on European stock exchanges during the time period 2020 to 2023. The purpose is to determine whether sin stocks yield abnormal returns during a period characterised by political and economic turmoil, compared to comparable utility stocks. To do so, sin portfolios are made on companies in the "Triumvirate of sin" which includes the tobacco, alcohol and gambling industry. The regression analysis applies the Fama-French three factor model to estimate portfolio alphas for each sin portfolio, the comparable portfolio, and the long-short portfolio, which takes a long position in sin stocks and a short position in comparable stocks. The study found no statistically significant over- or underperformance of sin stocks, which could be caused by the absence of factors that drive sin stock performance during the examined time frame. This suggests that investors may not have systematically favoured sin stocks as safe haven assets during the studied period. Despite the idiosyncratic characteristics of sin stocks, the performance was still influenced by overall market conditions, although sensitivity to the market decreased when executing a long-short investment strategy. The contrasting result from previous research underscores the variability in investor perceptions across different regions and time periods. Ultimately, the study provides insights into navigating economic and political uncertainty whilst capitalising on market conditions.

records.title: Unpacking Performance: A Comparative Study of Value-Added and Alpha Metrics in Predicting Swedish Mutual Fund Manager Performance
records.abstract: This study explores the usage of the gross alpha and value-added metrics to evaluate actively managed mutual fund manager performance in Sweden, inspired by the seminal research of Carhart (1997) and Berk & van Binsbergen (2015). By tailoring and combining their methodologies to the Swedish market, known for its unique investment culture, the paper aims to uncover the predictive power of these metrics in assessing such performance between 2006 and 2019. The empirical findings, derived from a comprehensive dataset from Morningstar Direct, reveal that the value-added measure offers a more precise prediction of mutual fund manager performance as compared to the gross alpha measure. However, the study also highlights the difficulty of definitively attributing fund performance to managerial skill, given the complex interplay of various factors influencing fund returns, coupled with the challenges of data collection inherent in focusing on such a narrowly defined geographical area. These insights contribute to the broader discourse on mutual fund management efficiency, especially within the context of the Swedish investment landscape.

records.title: Sustainability in Active Management: Short-term Implications of the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation
records.abstract: This paper provides a comparative analysis of the short-term implications on active management of equity mutual funds following the implementation of the European Union's Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR). We analyze how the short-term development in investor demand, fund size growth, performance, and managerial ability to generate value relate to the relative degree of sustainability objectives for each fund classification under the SFDR. We find that increases in investor demand and fund size growth are associated with higher sustainability-related objectives, along with implications of short-term effects of diminishing returns to scale for the relatively more sustainable funds. Following the SFDR implementation, we do not find that a higher degree of sustainability-related investment constraints has accentuated the effect of decreasing returns to scale in the short-term development. Our findings suggest that the average fund manager of the fund classification with the highest degree of sustainability objective has been the most skilled in navigating the implementation of the SFDR as this classification exhibits superior short-term development in the value extracted from the market.

records.title: Home Mortgage Constraints and Rental Market Frictions: Lessons from Norway
records.abstract: We investigate frictions in the housing market affecting the dynamics between the tenant- and owner-occupied parts of the market in a predominantly unregulated environment. We do this by analyzing the Norwegian housing market. Most prominently, we find data indicating that the tightened government-imposed down payment requirements of 2011 alter market dynamics and increase the pressure on the rental market. Subsequently, we argue that those households affected by mortgage constraints in general not only include low-income households but also high-income immigrant households with a lacking credit history. Furthermore, our findings suggest that some private information variables can explain the variation of rents and prices, although this is clearer for purchase prices than for rents.

records.title: Can Investors on Nasdaq Stockholm Interpret Percentages? Non-Proportional Thinking in a Swedish Setting
records.abstract: We further test the theory of non-proportional thinking. It refers to investors thinking about price changes of stocks in nominal terms rather than percentage terms following news events, which induces higher volatility for lower priced shares. Investors have been shown to engage in non-proportional thinking on U.S. stock exchanges, but it has not thoroughly been investigated outside the U.S. We study non-proportional thinking on the Swedish stock market, a country where financial literacy is among the highest in the world. In line with the theory, our results suggest that a doubling in share price leads to a decrease in volatility of around 10%. In the U.S., the equivalent result was a 20-30% decrease in volatility.

records.title: Hedging The Future: Diversification Benefits of Carbon Credits
records.abstract: Our study assesses the diversification benefits of EUA futures from 2008 to 2024, revealing modest market betas and high idiosyncratic risk, which can be mitigated through December futures contracts. By transferring risk to diversified investors, firms can gain large diversification benefits associated with carbon credits. Our analysis shows mostly positive beta values for EUA futures against the European markets, various industries, and commodities. We find that beta values are not tied to carbon intensity but rather to sector-specific demand cycles. Energy commodities linked to production also show higher beta values, indicating a stronger connection to EUA futures. The Beta's peaks during events such as the 2008 crisis and the 2020 pandemic highlight the sensitivity of EUA futures to market shocks, although the impact varies with different economic disruptions, with negative demand shocks found to have the largest impact.

records.title: The Smooth Transition: A Study on The Impact of the French Board Gender Quota on Firm Value
records.abstract: This study examines the impact of the French board gender quota on firm value, drawing comparisons with previous research. Utilizing methodology akin to Ahern and Dittmar (2012), who investigated the Norwegian board gender quota, we analyze the effects of the French quota enacted in 2011. We use the pre-quota cross-sectional variation in board gender diversity to instrument for exogenous changes to corporate boards resulting from the law. Contrary to prior findings on the impact of board gender quotas, our results reveal no evidence supporting the notion that the French quota negatively affects firm value. Despite the quota mandating an involuntary increase in female board members, we observe no significant impact on immediate stock return or long-term indicators such as Tobin's Q and return on equity. Additionally, board size and tenure remain unaffected by the quota, suggesting a smooth transition rather than forced adjustments. By comparing with the Norwegian experience, characterized by rushed compliance, we argue that the extended compliance period and softer sanctions upon failure to comply in France facilitated a gradual adjustment process, mitigating adverse effects on firm value. These results challenge prior assumptions and provide policymakers with insights on implementing gender quotas without compromising firm performance while advancing gender equality in corporate leadership.

records.title: Does Cybersecurity Risk Impact Stock Returns of Nordic Large Cap Firms?
records.abstract: In this study, we investigate the impact of cybersecurity risk on the stock returns of Nordic large-cap firms by employing textual analysis on firms' annual reports. Inspired by methodologies used in prior research on U.S. firms, we develop a cybersecurity risk score tailored to the Nordic market. We then create three cybersecurity risk-sorted portfolios and a long-short portfolio that goes long in low-risk cybersecurity stocks and short in high-risk cybersecurity stocks. Our findings indicate that cybersecurity risk does not impact Nordic large-cap stock returns, with any differences in the generated returns of our cybersecurity risk-sorted portfolios being explained by market risk, size, and value factors. Additionally, we provide descriptive evidence that larger firms with high price-to-book ratios are more likely to be subject to cyberattacks. Furthermore, we evaluate the cybersecurity risks of specific industries and how these risks have developed over time. Our study contributes to the growing field of research on cybersecurity's impact on financial assets and provides first-of-its-kind evidence in the Nordic market.

records.title: Gender at the Deal Table : A Study of Director Gender Impact in Mergers and Acquisitions
records.abstract: Does CEO gender help to explain merger and acquisition decisions? We examine the financial and investment strategies of female CEOs compared to male CEOs in the Nordic region by analysing both public and private M&A transactions. Female CEOs are significantly inclined to acquire targets with lower EV/EBITDA multiples. However, there is no significant difference between male and female CEOs concerning target leverage, book-value size ratio, and bid premium. These findings suggest that in a relatively gender-equal environment like the Nordics, discrepancies in M&A decisions between male and female CEOs are not prominent.

records.title: Household Response to Fiscal Stimulus: A Study on Japan's 2020 Special Cash Payments Scheme
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the effectiveness of Japan's 2020 Special Cash Payments Scheme, a fiscal response to mitigate the economic downturn caused by the COVID- 19 pandemic. Implemented as part of broader emergency economic measures, the government distributed ¥100,000 to every resident to maintain economic stability. Using data from the Family Income and Expenditure Survey, this study employs an Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression and an Instrumental Variable (IV) approach to analyse the short-term and long-term impacts of these payments on household financial behaviour. The findings reveal that while there was a significant immediate increase in household financial assets and a reduction in loans, the consumption response varied significantly depending on liquidity constraints and was more pronounced in non-liquidity constrained households. Additionally, the analysis suggests that the timing of the payments could have been optimised, as the payments were not fully utilised until economic conditions worsened. This study contributes to understanding the dynamics of fiscal stimulus on household behaviour during economic crises and provides insights for future policy formulation.

records.title: Leverage Constraints and the Beta Anomaly: Betting Against Beta in the Swedish Stock Market
records.abstract: We expand on prior research around the beta anomaly by examining whether the superior performance of low-beta stocks compared to high-beta stocks persists in the Swedish market from 2011 to 2023. Building on the work in "Betting Against Beta" by Frazzini and Pedersen (2014), we construct a market neutral Betting Against Beta (BAB) factor and evaluate its performance. We contribute to the literature by updating their research with the most recent data from Sweden, focusing on stocks listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, and examining the underlying economics of the beta anomaly. The findings reveal how portfolios of low-beta stocks yield higher and statistically significant alphas compared to high-beta stock portfolios over the sample period, highlighting a superior performance of low-beta assets. Consistent with Frazzini and Pedersen's results, we observe a significant positive alpha for a self-financing BAB portfolio during the tested period, suggesting a breach of the assumptions underlying traditional asset pricing models such as the CAPM. Furthermore, we analyze ownership data on stocks listed on Nasdaq Stockholm and identify that leverage- constrained investors are a key factor driving the overpricing of high-beta assets in Sweden. Additionally, we find that periods of tighter leverage constraints, as measured by a Swedish equivalent of the TED-Spread, negatively impact the short-term returns of a BAB portfolio while having no significant effect on long-term performance.

records.title: Developed vs. Developing: An event study on the stock price response to the issuance of green bonds in Sweden compared to China
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the market reactions to corporate green bond announcements in Sweden and China, employing an event study methodology within the framework of signaling theory and cost of capital considerations. The findings reveal distinct regional reactions: a positive response in Sweden indicates that the market perceives green bond issuances as credible signals of environmental commitment. Conversely, in China, the negative response could suggest market skepticism about the financial implications of such environmental initiatives. These differing reactions underscore the significance of regional economic contexts and cultural perceptions in sustainable finance. The study contributes to understanding the strategic implications of green finance, highlighting how investor perceptions can significantly impact the effectiveness of signaling through green bonds.

records.title: The Maturity Ambiguity: A Study on the Liquidity Premia in US Treasury Securities
records.abstract: This thesis explores the impact of strict mutual fund maturity constraints on the liquidity premium of US Treasuries by examining the yield spreads between assets of varying maturities and liquidity. We find that there is different demand dynamics depending on maturity of T-bills. In addition, the existence of an on-the-run phenomenon within the T- bill market is assessed, with no clear evidence that a consistent liquidity premium between these highly liquid assets exist. The drivers behind the liquidity premium between T-bills and deposits is studied with the opportunity cost of money being a dominant driver over time, that in recent years have had the T-bill supply alongside it as a contributor to the liquidity premium of near-money assets.

records.title: The Family Factor: Family Ownership and Firm Performance in the European Market
records.abstract: We study the impact of family ownership on firm performance within the STOXX Europe 600 index over the period 2010 to 2022. Using a sample of 577 firms, of which 98 are family-owned, we employ a two-way fixed effects OLS regression model to investigate the relationships between family ownership and two firm performance measures: stock return and return on assets (ROA). Our analysis differentiates between high and low levels of family ownership, as well as younger and older family firms, to assess performance nuances. The findings indicate that family-owned firms generally exhibit higher ROA than non-family firms, suggesting that family ownership contributes positively to firm profitability. Family-owned firms have higher stock returns over our studied period, however, we cannot deduce that it is the effect of family ownership. Additionally, we present evidence that higher family ownership significantly increases firm performance compared to lower family ownership.

records.title: Unveiling Market Seasonality: The Day-of-the-Week Effect on the Swedish Stock Market Across Different Market Conditions
records.abstract: This study explores the day-of-the-week effect on the Swedish stock market between 2014 and 2024. The day-of-the-week effect, a phenomenon where stock returns differ predictably depending on the weekday, poses a challenge to the Efficient Market Hypothesis. Our research examines variations in this effect across different market capitalizations and timeframes defined by the COVID-19 pandemic. The results reveal a pronounced day-of-the-week effect within Sweden's small- and mid-capitalization stocks. Further, our findings suggest that Friday returns are significantly higher than other days of the week for small- and mid-capitalization stocks, along with varying results for the different subsamples, indicating that market efficiency may fluctuate based on economic conditions and specific market capitalizations.

records.title: The Value of Values
records.abstract: This study examines the long- and short term relationship between ESG performance and financial performance, focusing on companies in the S&P 500 and S&P 500 ESG indices. Our findings suggest that there is no significant relationship between ESG- and financial performance, neither in the long- nor short term. However, when observing the individual components of ESG, firms with higher E scores perform worse financially, while firms with higher S scores perform better financially, in the long term. Also, firms in the S&P 500 ESG index generally have larger market capitalizations and outperform financially in the short term but not in the long term. Hence, the ESG index superior financial performance in the short term can partly be attributed to larger market capitalization, rather than ESG performance. However, the same cannot be concluded for the long term since larger market capitalization does not necessarily mean better financial performance, as proven by the comparison of the two indices.

records.title: The Effects of Political Connections on Firms' Abnormal Returns in Thailand
records.abstract: Developing economies experience significant political instability. Thailand, which has experienced 21 coup d'états since 1932, exemplifies this turbulence, particularly with the 2006 and 2014 coup d'états against the siblings Thaksin and Yingluck Shinawatra under the pretext of alleged nepotism. We exploit this unique historic incidence of two coups against prime ministers of the same family to investigate to what extent politically connected firms experienced abnormal high/low returns in periods ex ante and ex post the coups. We therefore combined the financial data, including firm characteristics and daily stock returns of approximately 450 Thai firms for each coup, and categorized them based on political connections, identified through an extensive manual-compiled dataset of politicians and their families.
