We find that in the majority of periods surrounding the events of 2006 and 2014, the effect of political connection remains insignificant. However, we suggest that political connections might exhibit periodic effects, particularly in times of drastic political instability, since politically connected firms experienced solely significantly higher negative abnormal returns than unconnected firms in the direct aftermath of these events. Therefore, our research contributes to understanding the dynamics of political connections in developing economies and the firm-level impacts of drastic political events.

records.title: Climate Crisis: Just Another Annual Report - An Impression Management Discourse Analysis of Organizational Decarbonization in Corporate Disclosures
records.abstract: This paper investigates the discursive strategies involved in communicating carbon targets, analysing 27 publicly available corporate reports of five major Swedish firms - Atlas Copco, Essity, H&M, Scania, & Skanska - from 2019 to 2023. This period captures the increasing adoption and standardisation of carbon emission reduction targets with respect to the disclosing firms. The analysis is framed by organizational discourse theory, applying an adjusted typology of impression management strategies (Dunne et al., 2021) to the firms' decarbonization communications. Four aggregate themes emerge from this analysis, conveying the following impressions: (1) We are climate leaders, (2) We have embarked on a climate journey, (3) We trust the science, and (4) Underperformance is not our fault - We will perform in the long term. Altogether, this study addresses the impression management research gap in carbon accounting, demonstrating the discursive strategies involved in communicating organizational climate work to stakeholders. Furthermore, these findings contribute to critical research understandings of the translational process of climate change in corporate disclosures.
records.lds04: Bachelor Thesis in Accounting and Financial Management

records.title: When Central Banks Speak: A Study on the Impact of Central Bank Announcements on the Swedish Stock Market
records.abstract: This thesis investigates how unexpected Swedish monetary policy announcements influence the stock market in Sweden. Using the Riksbank's high-frequency monetary policy event-study database (2004-2024) and daily industry indices from Nasdaq Nordic, we estimate the effects of these monetary shocks on the broad OMX Stockholm Price Index and on industry-level responses. Our results show that a 1-percentage-point unexpected increase in the 1-month SEK OIS rate leads to a decline of approximately 1.66% in the aggregate equity market index, robust across announcement types and outlier-adjusted specifications. Pure timing surprises deliver weaker, statistically insignificant effects, indicating a forward-looking channel in Sweden similar to the United States. We find little and insignificant cross-industry heterogeneity. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of the surprise component of Riksbank policy communication for Swedish asset prices and provide new evidence on monetary transmission in a small and open economy.

records.title: When does payment method lose its signaling power in M&A? - Evidence from market reaction
records.abstract: This paper examines whether payment method still conveys bidder negative information in modern M&A. Using a European M&A sample of 1716 observations from 2014 to 2024, we focus on short-term acquirer announcement return using [-1; +1] deal announcement date window to compare the value associated with cash- and equity-financed deals. We identify two opposing drivers of equity financing: a synergies-enhancing instrument and a negative signal of bidder overvaluation. Our univariate result shows equity-financed M&A is no longer underperforming cash-financed M&A, thus generating higher marginal CAR. Additionally, we interact the payment method with target listing status, deal geography, and industry relatedness to clarify the associated strategic motives behind cash/stock payment. We find that stock is rewarded in private/subsidiary, cross-border, and cross-industry deals, where it functions as a risk-sharing mechanism for synergies alignment. Meanwhile, in public, domestic, and intra-industry deals, equity-financing still plays its traditional role in signaling bidder misvaluation.

records.title: News and carbon premium return
records.abstract: First, we study stock returns and emissions using a panel of publicly listed U.S. firms from 2007 to 2024. We find that stocks of firms with higher emissions intensity (CO2 emissions scaled by revenue) earn lower returns, consistent with the negative carbon return premium literature. This result is robust when testing various model specifications. We also tested carbon premium based on various other emission variables such as emission levels and emission growth rate and found no robust significant results. Furthermore, we estimate monthly carbon premium for the period 2010 to 2024 to examine whether carbon premium can be explained by traditional risk factors. We find that the negative premium cannot be explained by the Fama-French five-factor model. Lastly, this study further examines news effects on carbon premium by testing whether climate-change news can predict the carbon premium. We find that climate-change news has a positive effect on carbon return premium, with regulatory risk news having a stronger effect than physical risk news.

records.title: The MAX Effect and Firm-Specific Attention: How Reversals Vary with Investor Focus
records.abstract: We examine the MAX effect, defined as the negative relation between extreme daily returns and subsequent stock performance, in Swedish equities from 2011 to 2024. We document a robust MAX effect in both portfolio sorts and firm-level return predictability. Using Google search volume as a proxy for firm-specific investor attention, we show that the effect varies across attention levels: MAX-related reversals arise when extreme returns coincide with abnormally low or moderate attention but disappear entirely when attention is abnormally high. Although firm-level regressions confirm that MAX predicts next-month returns, they do not detect systematic moderation by abnormal attention at the one-month horizon. Taken together, the results indicate that firm-specific attention is an important variable associated with whether reversals occur after salient price jumps, highlighting the broader role of attention in behaviorally driven return anomalies.

records.title: Fund manager gender and investment performance -  a study of Nordic mutual funds
records.abstract: This thesis examines whether fund manager gender influences mutual fund performance and risk-taking in the Nordic market, a region known for high gender-equality standards, yet still underrepresentation of women in asset management. Using a comprehensive Morningstar Direct dataset of 1,132 actively managed Equity, Fixed Income, and Allocation funds from 2014-2024, the study analyses gender effects through descriptive statistics, OLS regressions, CAPM alpha and beta, variance tests, and robustness checks. Performance is evaluated both across the full sample, as well as during the Covid-19 crisis to assess whether market turbulence amplifies behavioural differences. Results show that gender differences are category-specific rather than universal. In Equity funds, female managers outperform male managers on Sharpe ratios and CAPM alphas while exhibiting similar beta, and volatility differs significantly by gender only. Fixed Income funds reveal no meaningful gender-related differences, while Allocation funds show similar returns but higher beta among male managers. During Covid-19, female equity managers continue to outperform, reinforcing the robustness of the findings. Overall, gender appears to matter primarily in settings with high managerial autonomy, such as equity management, whereas more constrained mandates remain gender-neutral. The study adds evidence that gender-performance relationships are context-dependent and shaped by mandate flexibility and market conditions within the Nordic market.

records.title: Brand Power Meets Market Fear: A Downside Risk Perspective
records.abstract: Brand equity represents an important intangible asset, yet its link to market behavior in negative-return months remains insufficiently understood. Understanding whether brand equity mitigates this so-called downside risk has implications for valuation, portfolio construction and corporate strategy. Despite its attention in contemporary discussions, there is no overarching measure of both downside risk and brand equity. We apply a novel measure of brand equity and a threefold framework to measure downside risk. We find an association between brand equity and downside risk, depending on the measure of downside risk and the portfolio-weighting scheme. Further, we show that crises affect this relationship non-universally. Also, strong brands tend to lower B2C firms' risk and partly offset the inherent risk we identify of following a B2B strategy. We consider various robustness tests and show that they do not materially invalidate our key results.

records.title: Debt Refinancing and Cross-Market Spillovers Into Credit Spreads
records.abstract: This paper examines whether the timing of corporate debt maturities influences credit spread pricing and the transmission of refinancing stress across markets. Using U.S. firm-level data from 2002 to 2024, we study how refinancing intensity (RI), the share of debt maturing within three years, affects credit default swap (CDS) and corporate bond spreads. RI commands a significant premium in CDS markets once firm characteristics are controlled for, yet its influence on bond spreads is negligible. RI also fails to predict future changes in credit spreads, indicating that rollover exposure is priced only when conditions deteriorate. Residual refinancing risk factors that remove size, value, and bond-market liquidity show that refinancing stress originates in CDS markets and later reaches bonds, while equity signals are short-lived. Our results identify refinancing stress as a credit-market state variable, most clearly reflected in CDS spreads and only weakly visible in bond spreads or equity returns.

records.title: Taking the common currency out of the common market: Redenomination risk in the eurozone
records.abstract: This paper examines whether political and macroeconomic variables can explain and predict redenomination risk spreads, defined as the residual CR14-CR CDS premium derived through a synthetic-control method for France, Italy, and Germany between 2015 and 2024. Using daily CDS data combined with monthly political and macroeconomic indicators, we construct country-specific redenomination spreads that seeks to isolate the market-implied risk of a euro exit. We then run OLS regressions linking these spreads to inflation, output gaps, ECB policy rates, exchange rates, government debt, trade measures, and political variables. Our findings show that redenomination risk is highly country-specific and event-driven. Italy exhibits sensitivity to political variables such as parliamentary EU skepticism and election timing. Germany shows minimal redenomination risk, driven only weakly by government EU position, consistent with a safe-haven status and the possibility of negative redenomination premia. France demonstrates persistent positive redenomination spreads, but these are less well explained by observable political or macroeconomic determinants. Across countries, selected macroeconomic variables, particularly inflation and the EUR/USD exchange rate, provide additional explanatory power, though their effects vary by national context. Our results suggest that redenomination risk functions as a political tail-risk premium as it is dormant for long periods but prone to repricing around elections, coalition uncertainty, or institutional credibility shocks. These findings have practical implications for investors in sovereign debt, indicating that traditional economic credit models may miss relevant forward-looking risks unless they incorporate euro-membership credibility.

records.title: Intergenerational Wealth Mobility: How Policy Changes Affect Intergenerational Wealth Mobility in Sweden
records.abstract: We use a life-cycle simulation model based on Swedish administrative data to quantify how wealth taxation affects intergenerational wealth mobility. We find that a 1 percentage point increase in wealth tax reduces the mean wealth gap between the Very Rich and the Non-Rich by 6.2%. However, when we assign counterfactual behavioral parameters, risk aversion, time preference, and bequest motives, from the Non-Rich group to all socioeconomic groups, the effect of the tax drops to 0.2%. This shows that persistent wealth accumulation is primarily driven by inherited behavioral traits rather than inherited wealth alone and that the effect of wealth tax on wealth accumulation gaps is limited. Even under a flat 5% wealth tax, wealth accumulation among the Very Rich remains significantly higher. This suggests that while wealth taxation can reduce absolute disparities, long-run wealth persistence is primarily driven by behavioral differences rather than taxation alone.

records.title: Application of CatBoost for Credit Rating Prediction
records.abstract: Deep learning models have recently emerged as a promising approach to financial distress prediction. In particular, the CatBoost model-a gradient boosting algorithm optimized for categorical data-has shown promising results. This report evaluates the effectiveness of CatBoost in predicting active S&P credit ratings using financial data for public and private companies. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) is used to improve model interpretability and analyze feature importance, and SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique) is explored to address class imbalance. Results show that the model performs well, with most misclassifications occurring within one or two adjacent rating categories. Key predictors include categorical variables like sector and country, as well as financial ratios like net margin, return on equity, interest coverage ratio and debt-to-assets. Additionally, these findings offer some insight into the otherwise proprietary credit rating methodologies employed by rating agencies.

records.title: Debt Maturity, Firm Liquidity, and Equity Returns: European Evidence
records.abstract: This paper provides evidence that European firms that frequently refinance outstanding debt exhibit higher equity returns, but this premium is conditional on firm size and liquidity. We find that small firms that frequently rollover debt with a stable liquidity position have higher returns, whereas those with weaker liquidity face lower returns. The refinancing premium is consistent with greater exposure to rollover risk, a key risk for which equityholders demand compensation. Even so, refinancing when liquidity is constrained amplifies the risk of financial distress, reflected in a return discount rather than a premium. Our results suggest that corporate asset pricing should consider not only the maturity structure of debt but also its joint interplay with liquidity position and firm size.

records.title: Strength in Numbers: Reddit, Returns, and Rhetoric: Retail Investor Impact on Technology Stocks in a Politically Charged Market
records.abstract: This thesis investigates how retail investor sentiment on Reddit influences the performance of four big tech stocks (Tesla, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Apple) during a politically charged period. The analysis uses the Valence Aware and sEntiment Reasoner (VADER) for sentiment analysis, paired with daily stock data to capture the relationship between retail sentiment and stock returns, as well as trading activity. The study finds that sentiment has a generally weak and statistically insignificant correlation with daily stock returns of the chosen companies. However, the findings reveal stronger and more consistent relationships between sentiment and trading volume, particularly for Tesla, suggesting that sentiment may act as a behavioral trigger without consistently affecting prices. The study contributes to understanding the nuanced role of social sentiment in financial markets, particularly during periods of heightened political uncertainty.

records.title: Public Office, Private Gains (AN ANALYSIS OF PERFORMANCE BASED ON U.S. CONGRESS' STOCK TRADING DISCLOSURES)
records.abstract: By studying the stock transactions made by U.S. lawmakers, we find that members of Congress consistently earn abnormal returns on their stock trades, and that a value-weighted portfolio based on timely disclosure information (under the STOCK Act, 2012), also consistently would have generated statistically significant alpha during the period of 2012-2023. Disaggregating Congress by group characteristics, show that certain sub-groups of Congress have performed especially well and that the timing of disclosures has a close correlation with how valuable this disclosure information is for outside investors: longer delays correlate with larger interim returns, and trades reported on time generally outperform otherwise similar late-reported trades after disclosure.

records.title: CSR Under Pressure: An Analysis of CSR and Stock Returns in Europe During COVID-19
records.abstract: This paper investigates whether Corporate Social Responsibility shields firm value during and after exogenous shocks, using the COVID-19 crisis as a case study. The main focus is whether firms with higher CSR scores experienced better stock performance during the crisis and the following recovery period. The study analyzes a sample of 610 public European companies, applying regressions on raw and market-adjusted stock returns for the crisis (February 19th to March 25th, 2020) and post-crisis (March 25th to June 3rd, 2020) periods. The analysis includes control variables for firm financials, Fama-French factor loadings and industry fixed effects. During the crisis, CSR is positively associated with adjusted returns, but the effect disappears once controls are introduced. In the post-crisis period, CSR is negatively and significantly associated with both raw and adjusted returns. Idiosyncratic risk shows a strong positive relationship with post-crisis returns, indicating that firms with higher risk profiles outperformed in the recovery phase.

records.title: Does Past Performance Guarantee Future Returns? The Role of Fund Growth and Sector in Private Equity Performance Persistence
records.abstract: For investors in Private Equity (PE), the ability to identify persistent outperformers can significantly influence long term returns. In this paper we analyse performance persistence within PE using a comprehensive dataset containing both fund and deal level data; including 1004 funds managed by 419 general partners (GPs) and 36,292 deals across 755 GPs. We replicate the models in Harris et al. (2023) to measure persistence and extend them by looking at the role of sector and scaling. We find persistence over one and two fund cycles for both buyout and venture capital funds. Additionally, we find that excessive scaling negatively impacts the performance of buyout funds and that persistence diminishes when they scale above 200% over two fund cycles. Finally, we show that the existence of persistence varies depending on the sector or industry a GP invests in. These findings are useful to investors in deciding where to allocate their capital, showing that they should evaluate the past performance of PE firms as well as how they manage growth across fund vintages.

records.title: Different Minds, Better Returns? Investigating Diversity and Fund Performance in the Swedish Mutual Fund Market
records.abstract: Four easily observable characteristics - gender, university, academic major, and prior workplace - capture key differences in fund performance among Swedish mutual fund management teams. Using a panel dataset of Swedish actively managed equity funds, we compute team-level diversity scores and regress them on alpha and value added measures. We find that the relationship between team diversity and fund performance is dimension specific and sensitive to model specification. Diversity in academic majors emerges as the most statistically and economically significant predictor of superior fund performance. In contrast, teams whose managers attended differentiated universities underperform their homogeneous counterparts in terms of abnormal returns. In cross-sectional analyses, we find that gender diversity is negatively associated with fund performance, while workplace diversity shows no consistent effect on financial outcomes. These findings highlight that not all dimensions of diversity contribute equally to fund performance, with implications for fund selection and team composition.

records.title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Stock Returns: Assessing Emission Type, Firm Size, and Regional Differences
records.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and stock returns, addressing the ongoing debate over the existence of a carbon premium, namely, whether investors demand higher returns for holding fossil fuel-intensive stocks. Although research on this topic is expanding, results remain inconclusive, often due to variations in methodological approaches. First, we contribute to the existing literature by examining the baseline relationship between GHG emissions and stock returns, and by comparing vendor-estimated and reported GHG emissions. Second, we extend the literature by assessing the moderating effects of firm size and exploring regional differences between the U.S. and Europe based on the constructed models. Our findings support the evidence of a carbon premium for both reported and vendor-estimated emissions; however, the relationship remains sensitive to research design choices. We observe that firm size moderates the relationship, while evidence from the European sample is less statistically significant compared to that of the U.S.

records.title: When Good Firms Go Private: ESG Performance and Voluntary Delisting
records.abstract: This paper examines whether firm ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) performance influences voluntary delisting from public equity markets. Using a Cox Proportional Hazards model on a panel of over 3,200 public and private firms, we document a robust positive association: high-ESG firms have a significantly higher likelihood of voluntarily exiting public markets. We further exploit the EU's Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) as a quasi-exogenous ESG shock. A Difference-in-Differences analysis compares voluntary delisting rates of EU firms with matched US firms before and after the policy implementation. We find that post-NFRD, EU firms voluntarily delist at significantly lower rates relative to US firms, where this decline was driven by the top ESG performers. The result suggests that public listing and ESG profiles interact in complex ways: while high ESG firms are more prone to go private generally, disclosure mandates can mitigate this effect. These findings have important implications for policymakers and investors concerning the credibility of market-based ESG mechanisms and the design of disclosure regulations.

records.title: Private Equity Ownership In Times Of Crisis: Examining The Financial Resilience Of Swedish Private Equity-Backed Companies During The Covid-19 Crisis
records.abstract: Whether private equity (PE) ownership enhances or limits firm resilience during times of crisis has been explored in previous studies, particularly using data from British companies. To extend this research, we examine Swedish firms during the Covid-19 crisis, comparing the performance of PE-backed companies to that of closely matched non-PE-backed peers. Our analysis finds no statistically significant differences in financial resilience between the two groups during the pandemic. This contrasts with earlier UK-based findings and may reflect structural differences in national PE markets or the relatively milder economic impact and policy response in Sweden. However, the relatively small sample size in our study may have limited the ability to detect subtle but meaningful effects. These results highlight that the impact of PE ownership on crisis resilience is context-dependent and underscore the importance of region-specific research in understanding these dynamics.

records.title: Leading The Wallet: How Female Headship Shapes Household Financial Behaviour Across The Eurozone
records.abstract: This thesis investigates the drivers of female financial headship and its impact on household portfolio allocation across asset classes and gender-based normative contexts. We develop a two-stage utility maximisation model in which households assign financial headship based on observable financial potential and forward-looking expectations of investment performance, subject to gender norms. Using microdata from the European Central Bank's (ECB) Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS), we empirically test this framework and examine the impact of female headship on household financial investment decisions. First, we find that while female headship does not affect aggregate market participation or returns, it leads to distinct patterns across five core asset classes. Second, our results indicate that female headship is associated with lower financial literacy and reduced risk-taking. Finally, we show that financial behaviour and investment patterns systematically vary with a country's prevailing gender norms. These findings highlight the importance of gender equality and the broader normative context in shaping household financial decision-making.

records.title: Rollover Risk and Firm Productivity: Evidence from the 2008 Credit Crunch in the United States
records.abstract: This paper investigates whether refinancing pressures from the 2008 credit supply shock contributed to the post-crisis productivity slowdown among U.S. public firms. Exploiting the unexpected collapse of Lehman Brothers, we treat each firm's share of long-term debt maturing in 2008 as an exogenous proxy of rollover risk. Using a sample of 3,624 firms, we find that those with higher rollover risk experienced significantly larger declines in post-crisis total factor productivity (TFP) growth. A 10 percentage-point increase in rollover risk is associated with a 0.078 percentage-point larger decline in annual TFP growth. The causal interpretation is strengthened through a placebo test using the 2001 recession, in which rollover risk did not predict subsequent productivity. We also show that firms without credit rating, which typically lack bond-market access, were particularly vulnerable.

records.title: The Entrepreneurial Ecosystem of Kosovo: A Field Study of Local Startup Entrepreneurs
records.abstract: I explore the entrepreneurial ecosystem of Kosovo by analyzing the experiences and mindsets of 16 local startup entrepreneurs. Using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis based on Braun & Clarke's (2006) qualitative framework, I identify five key themes: structural barriers to entrepreneurship, cultural and psychological challenges, the global spread of Kosovo's diaspora, innovation in adversity, and entrepreneurial mindset and values. The findings highlight crucial external and internal challenges, such as an underdeveloped infrastructure and a cultural risk aversion, as well as intrinsic advantageous traits across the subjects, such as creativity and resilience. The themes are deeply interconnected, and suggest applications in the form of specific policy decisions and programs aimed at altering cultural perceptions. However, the findings are preliminary in the field and highlight the need for more extensive and targeted research.

records.title: When Active Pays Off: The Role of Active Share in Turbulent Markets
records.abstract: This paper examines the role of Active Share in Swedish equity mutual funds across varying market conditions. Using quarterly holdings and daily returns from the end of 2018 to the end of 2024, we compute Active Share for all-equity mutual funds domiciled in Sweden that invest in Europe and match them to appropriate benchmarks. We find no consistent relationship between Active Share and excess return throughout our sample period. However, during periods of elevated uncertainty, most notably the COVID-19 crisis, funds with high Active Share significantly outperform their benchmarks, while no such evidence exists for funds with lower Active Share. These results suggest that the relevance of Active Share is context-dependent and particularly significant in turbulent markets. Our findings imply that investors and fund managers should consider Active Share a meaningful indicator primarily during periods of heightened uncertainty.

records.title: Ho Ho Holdings
records.abstract: This paper studies the Holiday Effect in modern Nordic and U.K. stock exchanges between 2006 and 2024. The Holiday Effect refers to the empirical observation that stock returns are higher on the final trading day before stock market holidays compared to remaining trading days. We find mixed evidence when considering all public holidays for the indices: OMXS30, OMXC20, OMXH25, OSEBX, and FTSE100. When studying long holidays only - defined as Easter and Christmas - we find that stock returns are significantly higher across all markets on the final trading day. Long holidays are also associated with lower volatility and reduced trading volume. The findings challenge the traditional risk-return trade-off and points to non-fundamental, potentially behavioral, drivers of market behavior. Our study contributes to literature by studying geographies in the Nordics over a more recent timeframe.

records.title: ESG in the Storm - Linking ESG Ratings and Stock Performance During Market Distress
records.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between ESG ratings and stock performance during periods of market distress, focusing on the 2022 downturn driven by inflation, geopolitical conflict, and monetary tightening. Drawing on the methodologies employed by Lins et al. (2017) and Albuquerque et al. (2020), the analysis evaluates the effect of ESG ratings on realized returns, abnormal returns, and volatility across European and U.S. equities. Using a cross-sectional OLS regression model, we find that ESG ratings are significantly positively associated with abnormal and realized returns, and negatively associated with total volatility. When employing a pooled panel OLS regression framework to compare the 2022 crisis period with the non-crisis year 2021, we find no evidence that these effects are unique to crisis conditions. Furthermore, we study operational performance and stakeholder loyalty as potential explanatory variables for our findings, but find no statistically significant evidence. Lastly, we compare our primary results using Refinitiv Eikon and MSCI ESG ratings and do not find consistent outcomes, highlighting the lack of consensus across ESG rating providers and the methodological challenges associated with a ratings-based approach. Our findings affirm the financial relevance of ESG in market downturns, while highlighting limitations in current rating methodologies and the need for more objective ESG indicators in future research.

records.title: Does Size and Age Matter?
records.abstract: This paper investigates how family control influences firm performance in Swedish publicly listed companies, with a specific focus on how firm size and age moderate this relationship. The study contributes to the existing literature by shifting attention from family ownership to a novel definition of family control, while analyzing it in a unique institutional setting, Sweden, where dual-class shares allow families to retain voting control with proportionally lower ownership. Using a panel dataset of 284 Swedish firms from 2010 to 2023, the study employs pooled OLS regression models with year and industry fixed effects to examine both accounting-based (ROA, ROE) and market-based (Tobin's Q, stock return) performance outcomes. The results indicate that family control has a positive and significant effect on accounting-based performance, consistent with theories of stewardship and agency cost reduction. However, this positive effect is diminished in larger and older firms, supporting the notion that organizational complexity weakens family control's benefits. In contrast, no consistently significant relationship is found between family control and market-based performance measures, suggesting that investors may discount the value of family control, possibly due to perceived risks associated with ownership-control discrepancies.

records.title: This Is Not Financial Advice: Investigating The Predictive And Reactive Nature Of WallStreetBets Sentiment
records.abstract: In this paper, we develop a novel sentiment index (WSB) based on the frequency of bullish and bearish words occurring in finance-related comments on the WallStreetBets subreddit. We find that when WSB is high, same-day returns for the market, high minus low systematic risk portfolios and meme stock portfolios are low, and have been low for the three previous days. We find no evidence that WSB causes returns in the portfolios explored. Instead, WSB is found to be Granger caused by prior market and meme stock portfolio returns. When WSB is high, the VIX is likely to have increased in the previous days as well, suggesting that when markets expectations on future volatility is, and has been, high, sentiment is decreased on WallStreetBets. We further find a bilateral Granger causation relationship between WSB and VIX.

records.title: Vice and Value: Three Decades of Sin Stock Returns
records.abstract: This thesis studies the returns of publicly listed companies in controversial industries, commonly referred to as "sin stocks". Building on methods by Hong and Kacperczyk (2009) and extending the definition of sin stocks to include fossil fuels and defense, the analysis investigates abnormal returns of sin stocks in the financial markets in the US and developed Europe. Using daily return data from 1994 to 2025, the study implements time-series regressions using CAPM, Fama-French three-factor (FF3) and five-factor (FF5) models. Portfolios are constructed, which contain sin stocks in the long position and, in addition, sin stocks in the long position coupled with comparable industries in the short position. The result show positive abnormal returns for sin stocks in long-only and long-short portfolios across the two geographic regions. This finding challenges recent studies on sin stocks by Sagbakken and Zhang (2022) and Richey (2017) that provide evidence for non-significant abnormal returns using the Fama-French five-factor model. The results suggest that investor exclusion of sinful industries leads to market inefficiencies. Moreover, time variations in the sin stock premium indicate that these inefficiencies may be sensitive to exogenous factors such as economic and political conditions.

records.title: Exploring the Weather Effect: The Impact of Weather Factors on the Swedish Stock Market
records.abstract: This paper investigates the weather effect on the Swedish stock market. It focuses on how weather conditions impact stock market returns, volatilities and trading volumes over the period from 1984 to 2024. The analyzed weather variables include temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, barometric pressure, wind speed, cloud coverage and sunshine time, and are all collected from the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute. Some evidence is found for Stockholm weather impacting stock market returns and volatilities. However, these effects generally seem to have diminished over time, perhaps as a result of markets becoming more efficient and globalized. Stronger evidence is found for weather impacting trading volumes. This study contributes to the literature by exploring the development of the weather effect over time in a previously relatively unexplored market.

records.title: Analyst Recommendations and Gender: Measuring the Performance of Newspaper Stock Recommendations
records.abstract: This study measures the effect that stock recommendations published by financial newspapers can have on actual stock prices and how that effect depends on the gender of the person making the recommendation. We construct a dataset with 3170 stock recommendations published by the Swedish financial newspaper Dagens Industri over three years and find evidence that recommendations have a direct effect on short-term stock returns and that this effect is stronger if the recommendation was made by a man, even after controlling for stock characteristics. One year after each recommendation, the stock had on average underperformed the benchmark index and no significant differences between male and female recommendations can be observed, further suggesting that the initial differences in price movements depend on how readers perceive the articles rather than differing abilities in predicting stock returns.

records.title: Do Patents Pay Off? A Study of the Patent-Performance Relationship in Sweden
records.abstract: We build on the study of Taglialatela & Barontini (2024) by analyzing how the different stages of the patenting process - filing and granting - affect firm performance in Sweden. Using firm-level data, we test the external validity of their findings on Italian SMEs and extend their study by examining heterogeneous effects across firm sizes. Applying staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) and triple-difference (DDD) estimators, we find that filing without securing a grant is associated with reduced turnover growth across all firm groups. In contrast, obtaining a patent grant yields significant revenue gains for SMEs, while large firms experience no such gains and exhibit lower profitability post-grant. We challenge the assumption that larger firms capture greater patent returns, and instead suggest that SMEs are better positioned to leverage grants through external signaling. We further highlight the role of policy and capital markets in shaping performance outcomes across the patenting stages. Our findings suggest that the economic value of intellectual property is not uniform, but contingent on firm-level characteristics and the broader institutional context.

records.title: Information Uncertainty and the Likelihood of Corporate Takeovers: Evidence from U.S. Public Firms
records.abstract: This thesis investigates whether information uncertainty influences the likelihood of acquisition among publicly listed firms in the United States. Drawing on theories of asymmetric information and valuation frictions, we examine whether firms characterized by higher uncertainty, which is proxied by idiosyncratic return volatility, forecast dispersion, and R&D-based development stage status, are systematically less likely to become takeover targets. Using a panel dataset of over 29,000 firm-year observations, comprising acquisition data for deals completed between 2015-2024, and applying logistic regression models, we find that firms with higher idiosyncratic volatility and those classified as development-stage are significantly less likely to be acquired. In contrast, forecast dispersion does not predict acquisition likelihood, suggesting that not all proxies capture uncertainty in ways relevant to acquirer behavior. Follow-up analyses show that development-stage firms are more likely to be acquired by strategic and foreign buyers, indicating that certain acquirer types may be better equipped to evaluate or exploit uncertain targets. These findings contribute to the M&A literature by highlighting how information frictions shape not only deal outcomes, but also the ex ante selection of acquisition targets.

records.title: Public Office, Private Gains? An Event Study on U.S. Congressional Stock Trades
records.abstract: This thesis examines whether members of Congress earn abnormal returns on their investments and under what conditions such returns might arise. Using a dataset of 41 851 stock transactions between 2012 and 2024, we use an event study methodology complemented by calendar-time portfolio regressions and sub-sample analyses. After adjusting for risk using the Fama-French Three-Factor model, we find no consistent evidence that congressional buy trades outperform the market on aggregate, while sale transactions show limited but statistically significant loss avoidance. However, sub-analyses reveal evidence of significant abnormal returns under specific conditions. Firstly, some congressional committees earn abnormal returns during crisis periods such as COVID-19 and the Russia-Ukraine invasion and trading stocks aligned with members' committee jurisdiction. Furthermore, we find limited support of market reaction on disclosures of congressional trades by high-profile members. These findings indicate that although legislation may have reduced broad insider trading, outperformance in certain conditions suggest that informational advantages may exist, raising implications for market fairness and the adequacy of current regulations.

records.title: Political Uncertainty and Corporate Investment in Sweden: How Uncertainty Related to Swedish General Elections Affect Corporate Investment in Swedish Public Firms
records.abstract: This study examines the impact of political uncertainty, caused by general elections, on corporate investment in Sweden. Using panel data from publicly listed firms between 1983 and 2024, we estimate a fixed-effects investment-Q model to analyze investment behavior around elections. While corporate investment in the overall sample does not show a significant reduction, our subsample analysis reveals significantly reduced investment in politically sensitive industries, under specific incumbent government ideologies and during periods of corporate tax policy changes. These results indicate that, in a coalition-based parliamentary system, the economic impact of election-related uncertainty is concentrated to firms with greater exposure to political decision-making.

records.title: The Signaling Effect of Share Repurchases: Short- and Long-Run Evidence from the Swedish Market
records.abstract: This paper examines 458 open market share repurchase announcements by Swedish firms from 2010 to 2019. Using a cumulative abnormal return (CAR) methodology, we find significant short-run abnormal returns averaging 1.02%, with stronger effects for small firms and value stocks. In the long-run, we observe a one-year average CAR of 8.24%, consistent with the Underreaction Hypothesis (UH) developed by (Ikenberry, Lakonishok, & Vermaelen, 1995). However, results beyond the one-year horizon and across firm characteristics are inconclusive and model-dependent. Our findings contribute to the literature of repurchase signaling in a modern, Swedish context, suggesting persistent market underreaction.

records.title: Studying the impact of Top Marginal Income Taxes on Income Inequality
records.abstract: This study examines the relationship between top marginal state income tax rates and income inequality across 35 U.S. states from 1990 to 2020. It employs a panel dataset and fixed effects regression models, the study tests whether higher top marginal tax rates are associated with lower Gini coefficients, controlling for state-wise factors such as union density, unemployment, and state revenue. The results show that progressive taxation is modestly but consistently linked to reduced income inequality, particularly when labour institutions and fiscal capacity are considered. These findings highlight that while tax progressivity remains an important redistributive tool, its consequences depend on broader institutional and structural dynamics.

records.title: Payout Choices: A Comparative Study of the Impact of Share Repurchase and Dividend Increase Announcements on Abnormal Returns in Sweden
records.abstract: This thesis uses a dataset of dividend increase announcements and share repurchase announcements in Sweden between 2000 and 2019 to investigate their comparative impact on short-term market reactions by estimating cumulative abnormal return over short-run event windows and long-term stock performance by calculating buy- and-hold abnormal returns over longer horizons. Our findings show that firms announcing dividend increases exhibit stronger and more significant average short- term cumulative abnormal returns in windows around the announcement compared to firms announcing buybacks. In our buy-and-hold abnormal return analysis, we find both announcement types to show significant and in similar magnitude abnormal returns in the long-term windows following the announcement. This finding suggests an initial market underreaction for both types of announcements, especially buybacks, with a gradual incorporation into stock prices over time. Further, using a panel data regression with fixed effects for firms and time, we find leverage, assets, and valuation at the time of announcement to be firm characteristics that strongly relate to long-run abnormal returns for both announcement types.

records.title: The Impact of Mergers on Corporate Innovation: Evidence from Decades of Patent Activity
records.abstract: This paper revisits the long-standing question of whether mergers stimulate or stifle innovation activity. The dataset comprises 4,767 completed U.S. mergers and 1,654 withdrawn attempts announced from 1980 to 2018, resulting in 58,476 firm-year observations within balanced five-year windows. We construct three core innovation outcomes that capture innovation scale, innovation novelty, and private value of innovations. We find that merger completion reduces the scale of target-firm innovation, measured by the quantity of generated patents, and also reduces the novelty, measured by citation intensity of patents. However, private value, deduced from abnormal stock-market returns, market anticipation, and adjusted for inflation using the CPI, increases for target firms. Our findings pertaining to acquirers show that their innovation output improves across the board, over the full period studied. We show that the aggregate effect of mergers on innovation is nuanced and provide novel insights on different aspects, which are broadly consistent with the existing literature. Our findings are relevant for antitrust enforcement, the allocation of resources within internal capital markets, and the strategic design of post-merger R&D integration.

records.title: Wartime Wallets: Assessing the Firm-Level Impact of the Post-2001 Fiscal Spending Shock
records.abstract: Major shifts in government spending can transform corporate behavior, but not always in predictable ways. Following the sharp rise in U.S. defense spending after 9/11, we use panel data and a difference-in-differences strategy to assess how this fiscal shock affected defense contractors relative to other firms between 1998 and 2005. While contractors experienced significant revenue growth, this did not translate into higher profitability or job creation. Larger firms responded by increasing capital investment, whereas smaller firms accumulated cash reserves. These differences highlight the role of firm characteristics in shaping responses to fiscal stimulus and carry important implications for the design of policies aimed at encouraging productive investment.

records.title: The Power of Indices: A Study of Joiners and Leavers to the Most Prominent Indices in the Nordics and Baltics
records.abstract: This paper investigates the index effect in the Nordic and Baltic stock markets through an event study on the five major indices: OBX, OMXB10, OMXC20, OMXH25 and OMXS30, covering the period 1996 to 2024. We find positive (negative) abnormal returns for inclusions to (exclusions from) the indices , in line with prior findings. The index effect refers to the abnormal returns and trading volumes observed when stocks are added to or removed from an index. This phenomenon has gained renewed attention with the global shift from actively managed to passively managed funds, which has heightened the role of indices in investment strategies. Utilizing an event study methodology, this research provides evidence consistent with the index effect. The study contributes to the literature by offering a comprehensive analysis of less-explored Nordic and Baltic markets.

records.title: The Impact of Geopolitical Risk on Firm Behavior and Stock Returns
records.abstract: We adopt established textual analysis methods to create the first validated firm level measure of geopolitical risk. We analyze the distribution of geopolitical risk across firms and the impacts of geopolitical risk exposure on firm actions and stock prices. We find evidence that, although firms are concerned about aggregate geopolitical risk, they may be more concerned about firm-specific geopolitical risk exposure. Further, we find evidence for the conclusion that geopolitical risk is negatively associated with capital expenditures and sales growth, and positively associated with stock price volatility. Finally, we find that portfolios consisting of firms with high geopolitical risks outperform portfolios of other firms in terms of abnormal returns.

records.title: The Price of Emissions: Decoding Green Returns
records.abstract: This study investigates how carbon emissions affect stock returns among Nasdaq OMX Nordic 120 companies, and how transparency in emissions reporting impacts this relationship. We find significant negative effects of scope 1 and 2 emissions on stock returns, controlling for size, book-to-market, and other known stock return predictors, implying that firms can increase financial returns by lowering emissions. For our main cross-sectional regression sample, we find no significant effects of scope 3 emissions, the emission growth rate of any scope, or the emission intensity of any scope on stock returns. Furthermore, we find that the negative effects of carbon emissions on stock returns seem to be driven by companies with non-transparent emissions reporting, and that a firm can mitigate the negative impact of carbon emissions on stock returns by increasing reporting transparency. Our results highlight the need for firms to consider their environmental impact and reporting standards in operating decisions.

records.title: Adaptive Makets and Attention-Driven Anomalies in Times of Crisis: A COVID-19 Perspective
records.abstract: This study examines the impact of day-of-the-week effects, specifically Fridays, on post-earnings announcement drift (PEAD) in the U.S. stock market from 2016 to 2023, with a specific focus on the COVID-19 pandemic period. Our findings reveal significant challenges in isolating the effects of investor inattention from firm-specific characteristics and the strategic timing of earnings announcements. While previous literature, such as DellaVigna and Pollet (2009), attribute anomalies like reduced Friday reactions to investor inattention, our results suggest that these patterns may instead arise from unobserved biases and external market factors. During the COVID-19 pandemic, shifts in market dynamics were observed, however, the evidence remains inconclusive regarding the persistence of traditional anomalies. Our analysis underscores the methodological challenges posed by non-random announcement distributions and selection biases, complicating the attribution of observed trends to specific behavioral or market inefficiencies. These limitations constrain the ability to draw definitive conclusions for market participants, highlighting the need for future research to explore broader datasets, alternative market contexts, and randomized announcement tests to address these issues. As financial markets are expected to face increasing volatility due to the growing likelihood of pandemics and similar systemic disruptions, understanding these dynamics is crucial for researchers, investors, and corporate managers.

records.title: Deals on Hold: A Study on the Impact of Policy Uncertainty on Merger and Acquisition Activity in Sweden
records.abstract: Policy uncertainty is significantly negatively correlated with merger and acquisition (M&A) activity in Sweden. Consistent with the real options channel theory, the effect is weaker in competitive industries, where delays are costly, and stronger in industries sensitive to government spending, where uncertainty about future profitability is greater. However, we find no evidence that irreversibility amplifies this effect. The negative effect is lasting, with no indication that delayed deals are completed later, highlighting the long-term costs of policy uncertainty for corporate investments.

records.title: NAVIGATING FINANCIAL DISTRESS: THE IMPACT OF FINANCIAL LITERACY ON HOUSEHOLD-LEVEL BANKRUPTCY
records.abstract: This study explores the protective role of financial literacy in reducing household financial distress, focusing on bankruptcy risk. Using data from the 2022 Survey of Consumer Finances, financial literacy is assessed via the "Big 3" questions and analyzed through linear, threshold and mediation models. Results show a significant negative relationship between financial literacy and bankruptcy, with the highest literacy levels offering the most protection, while intermediate scores have limited benefits. Subgroup analyses reveal that younger age groups, lower income groups and high debt-to-income groups benefit most from literacy improvements. The mediation analyses identify homeownership and credit card management as key behavioral pathways. While financial literacy strongly reduces bankruptcy risk, its effect on foreclosure is less pronounced, influenced more by structural and socio-demographic factors. These findings highlight the need for targeted financial education to support vulnerable populations and inform policy.

records.title: Guilty Profits: Does the Market Reward the Unethical?
records.abstract: This paper examines the performance of U.S. sin stocks - alcohol, tobacco and gambling - over the period 1965-2023, focusing on risk-adjusted abnormal returns. Using time-series regression across the CAPM, Fama-French Three-Factor model, Carhart Four-Factor model, and Fama-French Five-Factor model we find that sin stocks generate significant abnormal returns, with a monthly alpha of 42 basis points under the Fama-French Five-Factor model. Industry-level analysis finds that while all sin industries exhibit positive abnormal returns over the full period, only alcohol stocks maintain significance during 2007-2023, a time marked by heightened ESG adoption. However, findings from a placebo test suggest that the sin stock classification and its associated premium is influenced by random noise. This challenges the robustness of the sin premium and its attribution to systematic factors or social norms.

records.title: Music Sentiment and Stock Returns in Sweden
records.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between music sentiment, a novel proxy for investor sentiment, and stock returns in Sweden. We utilise Spotify data and calculate the stream weighted average valence (SWAV) for each week in our dataset to measure aggregate sentiment. This paper extends prior research by incorporating a longer time frame, firm-specific returns and cross-industry analysis to deepen the understanding of sentiment-driven dynamics. Our results reveal a significant positive relationship between music sentiment and concurrent stock returns on the market and firm level, with evidence of subsequent price corrections the following week. At the firm level, our findings reveal that this relationship is evident regardless of industry. Further cross sectional analysis indicate that riskier, high growth and financially distressed firms exhibit heightened sensitivity to sentiment. However, these findings cross sectional findings lack robustness and calls for further research. Sweden provides an ideal setting for this analysis, given its high retail investor participation and widespread Spotify usage, which enhance the reliability of sentiment as a market indicator.

records.title: Do Activist Types Matter? A Comparative Analysis of Shareholder Activists
records.abstract: Using a comprehensive dataset of 2,640 activist interventions from 2000 to 2022, we categorize shareholder activists into seven distinct activist types to examine potential heterogeneity among activists. We find that activist types select different target firms based on size, profitability, and payout policies. Hedge funds, private equity, venture capital, mutual funds, and other financial institutions generate significant positive abnormal returns of 5% around activism announcements. In contrast, interventions by pension funds and individuals result in significantly lower returns. Despite these initial differences, we observe convergence in firm performance across activist types over a one-year period. This suggests that although activist type impacts short-term market reactions, it does not determine long-term firm outcomes.

records.title: Unveiling the Puzzle of ESG Investing: An Analysis of ESG-Efficient Frontiers Across U.S. Macroeconomic Periods
records.abstract: We examine the interaction between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors and stock performance in the U.S. from 2002 to 2022, with a focus on analysing the differences between periods of economic expansions and recessions. Using a dataset of S&P 500 constituents, we construct ESG-Sharpe ratio (SR) frontiers based on the framework proposed by Pedersen et al. (2021). Our analysis of expansions reveals that the benefit of incorporating ESG information in portfolio selection diminishes over time, while the cost of non-pecuniary ESG preferences increases. However, we are unable to clearly assess similar effects during recessions, mainly due to the randomness of outcomes observed in those periods.

records.title: Independence in an Era of Interference: A Quantitative Exploration of the Relationship between Central Bank Independence and Inflation
records.abstract: By the end of the 20th century, central bank independence (CBI) had become an entrenched principle of monetary policymaking across many market economies worldwide. This rested on the belief that CBI provided a credible solution to the time-inconsistency problem in controlling inflation. However, CBI has become increasingly contested since the global financial crisis. Rising political interference and concerns over the role of central banks in macroprudential oversight and democratic accountability have challenged the assumed legitimacy of CBI. These developments create a rationale for reevaluating the empirical foundations for CBI. Much of the influential research on the relationship between CBI and inflation relies on limited empirical methods and data predating key macroeconomic shifts, and the overall findings are inconclusive. This paper reexamines the relationship between CBI and inflation with updated data and an improved methodological approach. Using panel data for 155 countries from 1963 to 2023, the relationship between CBI and inflation is estimated through an OLS model with extensive robustness measures, complemented by an instrumental variable specification that instruments CBI with accession to the Maastricht Treaty. Across specifications, the findings are consistent with the logic that independence reduces inflation. The findings strengthen the case for central bank independence as a means of maintaining low inflation and suggest that international frameworks, such as the Maastricht Treaty, can play a crucial role in facilitating its adoption.

records.title: Finance, Innovation, and Comparative Advantage: Financial Development and International Trade in Finance Dependent and Innovation Dependent Industries - A Global Perspective
records.abstract: We find that financial development is a key enabler in comparative advantage in international trade, in finance and innovation dependent industries. Countries with well-functioning financial institutions better enable firms that are dependent on external funding and innovations. Furthermore, the level of comparative advantage in finance dependent industries is largely attributed to an underlying innovation dependence. We use a model of Ricardian comparative advantage originally developed by Costinot (2009) and calibrate industry-level innovation dependence following Sampson (2023), to explain our findings. We primarily use data from OECD STAN and ANBERD databases and US Compustat databases.

records.title: Testing the Waters: Double Announcements in Swedish Rights Issues
records.abstract: In recent years, a new model for conducting rights issues has gained popularity on the Swedish Nasdaq Markets. This entails splitting the traditional announcement of a rights issue and its terms into two steps: an initial press release disclosing all terms except the subscription price and the number of shares to be issued, followed by a press release disclosing all terms. This study seeks to assess the difference in abnormal returns between firms conducting one or two announcements. The dataset is composed of 370 rights issues from the Swedish Nasdaq Markets (Nasdaq Stockholm and Nasdaq First North Growth Market) identified from the prospectus register of the Swedish Financial Supervisory. 302 of these fall under a single announcement occasion and 68 are executed with double announcements. We find significant evidence suggesting a negative market reaction in connection with the second announcement, despite the existence of a previous announcement. The announcements of full terms including subscription price and the number of shares issued are relevant to the market. We also find that in the case of double announcements, the short-term market reaction to the second press release is more negative for issues without any prior announcement of their intention. In other words, the first announcement precedes a smaller second price drop, suggesting a potential mitigating role. Consequently, we speculate that the initial press release can serve as a tool to facilitate the negotiations between the issuing company and its financial advisor regarding the terms of the rights issue, especially in companies with a thin shareholder base in terms of financial capacity. Testing the waters in this way through two announcements is of particular importance during times of strained financial markets.
records.lds04: Bachelor Thesis in Accounting and Financial Management

records.title: Do Environmental Leaders Perform Better During Disasters? - Evidence from the 2025 California Wildfires
records.abstract: On the 7th of January 2025, multiple wildfires broke out in the US state of California. Like other severe disasters, these fires affected society in many aspects. This study investigates one such effect: its impact on the American stock market. More specifically, we look at whether the environmental performance of S&P 500 firms played a deciding role in how the market treated firms' stocks in the time following the wildfires. The study conducted mean comparison tests and multiple linear regressions to identify whether a significant relationship existed between environmental performance and Cumulative Abnormal Returns (CARs). We investigated three separate time frames to account for differing reactions in different stages of the post-disaster period. We find no significant relationship in the short- or medium-term. Long-term results are mixed, with some models showing no effect and others showing a weak positive relationship. The long-term effect remains uncertain and requires further research to be fully understood.
records.lds04: Bachelor Thesis in Accounting and Financial Management

records.title: Beyond Speculation: Can Fundamental Blockchain Metrics Predict Token Returns?
records.abstract: We construct a three-factor model based on the cryptocurrency market, momentum, and transactions per user, which captures the cross-sectional returns of Layer 1 blockchains' native tokens. We replicate Liu, Wu, and Tsyvinski's (2022) methodology on a more recent and delineated sample and extend it to fundamental blockchain metrics. We construct zero-investment long-short portfolio strategies based on these characteristics, of which 26 are found to deliver statistically significant excess weekly returns. We show that all but two out of these strategies are explained by our three-factor model and discuss potential explanations for the significance of a fundamental-based factor. Finally, we construct a market regime analysis and find a bull market effect, which magnifies the excess weekly returns of all previously significant strategies.
records.lds04: Bachelor Thesis in Accounting and Financial Management

records.title: Mispriced and Misunderstood? The Impact of Liquidity on Tracking Errors in European ETFs
records.abstract: This thesis investigates how liquidity affects tracking errors in European passive ETFs. To examine this relationship, we apply panel regressions with fixed effects and double-clustered standard errors, controlling for return volatility and fund characteristics. Based on a sample of 494 ETFs from 2000 to 2024, we find that lower liquidity - measured by the relative quoted half spread - is strongly associated with higher pricing-based tracking errors, particularly weakening the price alignment between ETF market prices and their Net Asset Values (NAVs). This finding supports earlier evidence while extending it to the European ETF market. In contrast, tracking errors between NAVs and benchmark indices appear less sensitive to liquidity. The results highlight the importance of market liquidity for ETF pricing efficiency and underscore the challenges posed by Europe's fragmented trading landscape.

records.title: Zookeeping: A Comparison of Factor Pruning Methods
records.abstract: The proliferation of proposed risk factors in empirical asset pricing, often referred to as the factor zoo, complicates the identification of a true stochastic discount factor (SDF). To address this, we assess in- and out-of-sample cross-sectional performance for Fama-French models, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Risk-Premium PCA (RP-PCA), Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA), and a nonlinear Deep Latent Factor Model (DLFM) across varying regularization regimes. We find that the performance of dense and latent factor models depends strongly on the choice of regularization method and strength, and that the optimal choice of least-squares method itself depends on how factors are constructed, while a regularization-agnostic BMA model provides robust pricing of the cross-section. Finally, we find a positive relationship between model dimensionality and cross-sectional pricing ability; however, performance improvements diminish rapidly for latent factor models, suggesting that the underlying SDF is likely to be dense in observable factors, yet adequately represented by a relatively small set of latent factors.

records.title: Predetermined Demand: How Past Birth Cohorts Predict Regional House Price Growth in Sweden
records.abstract: In a panel of 20 Swedish counties observed annually from 1996 to 2022, the share of newborns in a county 27 years earlier is associated with subsequent five-year house price growth: a one standard deviation increase corresponds to about 4.7 percentage points of cumulative growth. The same lagged birth share predicts four housing-market outcomes at different horizons, with apartment prices peaking at lag 24, house prices at lag 27, transactions at lag 30, and construction at lag 32. Tracing the same cohort at successive ages from birth through home-buying age, birth-time location is a more reliable predictor of regional house prices than the cohort's location at any later age, and predictive power weakens sharply through the university years.

records.title: What the Market Reads: How EU Disclosure Harmonization Reshaped the Pricing of Swedish IPO Prospectuses
records.abstract: This paper studies whether the EU Prospectus Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 changed the way Swedish IPO prospectuses are written, and whether these changes affect first-day underpricing. We analyze 269 Swedish IPOs between 2006 and 2026 and use the textual decomposition method from Hanley and Hoberg (2010) to separate the prospectus language into standard and informative content. The results indicate that the Regulation did not mechanically increase firm-specific disclosure once firm characteristics, year effects, and industry effects are accounted for. We also find no clear unconditional relationship between prospectus content and first-day underpricing in the Swedish setting. However, joint Wald F-tests of the content × regulation interaction terms indicate that the Regulation changed how the market prices disclosure - particularly for the Total Document (F = 5.319, p < 0.001) and the Risk Factors section (F = 3.621, p < 0.01) - suggesting that the Regulation affects pricing not only by changing what issuers disclose, but also by altering how investors interpret disclosure.

records.title: Beyond Borders and Institutional Constraints: U.S. Equity Cross-listing and Refinancing Risk in Emerging Market Firms
records.abstract: Examining U.S. cross-listings across 25 emerging markets between 1988 and 2024, this paper provides evidence that firms experience a reduction in refinancing risk following an equity cross-listing on a U.S. exchange. The effect emerges gradually and persists over time. Over-the-counter listings show smaller and short-lived effects concentrated around the listing event, while private placements show no detectable impact. Extending the analysis to institutional heterogeneity, the reduction associated with exchange listings is concentrated in countries with weaker disclosure requirements and debt enforcement, where the institutional gap relative to U.S. standards is largest. Although the underlying mechanisms cannot be fully identified, exchange listings appear to relax financing constraints along a non-price dimension, with benefits substituting for weak home-country institutions.

records.title: Pricing the Unseen: How Intangible Assets Affect Investor Reactions to Payment Choice in Public M&A
records.abstract: This paper investigates whether target intangible asset intensity moderates the well-documented stock-payment discount in bidder announcement returns for acquisitions of publicly traded targets. In particular, the analysis examines whether stock payment functions as a risk-sharing mechanism under valuation uncertainty. Using data on public U.S. mergers and acquisitions from 2000 to 2022, the results confirm the persistence of a stock-payment discount. However, no robust evidence is found that this discount is attenuated for targets with higher intangible intensity. These findings suggest that, in acquisitions of publicly traded targets, target intangible asset intensity does not materially influence how investors interpret the choice of payment. Accordingly, stock payment does not appear to function as a risk-sharing mechanism in this setting. Overall, the paper contributes by providing updated evidence on the stock-payment discount and by examining whether target-side valuation uncertainty, proxied by intangible asset intensity, helps explain variation in bidder announcement returns.

records.title: When Similarity Sells and Diversity Delivers: The Dual Preferences Driving Mutual Fund Flows
records.abstract: Which characteristics shape investor demand for ESG mutual funds? Beyond performance, fees, and adherence to conventional investment strategies, we examine whether investors reward funds that adhere to the ESG strategies described in their prospectuses. Using SEC prospectus text, CRSP mutual fund data, and portfolio holdings for actively managed U.S. equity mutual funds from 2016 to 2024, we classify funds by ESG language in their Principal Investment Strategy sections and measure portfolio adherence to both conventional strategy peer groups and ESG-strategy peer groups. We show that fund flows increase when funds remain close to the average holdings of their conventional strategy peers, but not when ESG funds remain close to the average holdings of their ESG peers. Using idiosyncratic industry return shocks as instruments, we find suggestive evidence that investors may even prefer ESG funds that differentiate themselves from their ESG peer-group consensus. Our results uncover dual investor preferences in mutual fund flows: similarity sells in conventional strategy space, while diversity delivers in ESG strategy space.

records.title: Intangible Capital & Corporate Cash Holdings: International Evidence
records.abstract: Corporate cash holdings have risen over the past four decades, alongside firms' growing reliance on intangible capital. Because intangible capital is hard to pledge as collateral, this reliance lowers debt capacity and raises the demand for precautionary cash. We ask whether this intangible-collateral channel, originally documented for the United States, accounts for cash holdings internationally. We quantify its contribution by calibrating a dynamic structural model country by country across four advanced and four emerging economies. In the advanced economies, the channel accounts for an average of 55% of the increase in cash holdings. In the emerging economies, the evidence is weaker and does not support the same conclusion. Across countries, differences in intangible capital account for roughly half of the dispersion in cash levels, a contribution comparable to all other country-specific parameters combined. The evidence points to intangible capital being a central driver of corporate cash holdings across advanced economies.

records.title: Green Window Dressing in European ESG Funds
records.abstract: This study examines the prevalence of green window dressing among EU-domiciled SFDR Article 9 equity mutual funds. Green window dressing refers to the practice of temporarily adjusting fund holdings around disclosure dates to present a more sustainable portfolio to investors. Building on the methodology of Parise and Rubin (2025), this study uses return gap analysis and ESG beta comparisons to identify abnormal trading around disclosure dates and whether it serves to overstate ESG exposure. We document a significant return gap, consistent with disclosure-related trading. However, this trading does not reflect a significant change in ESG exposure. Contrary to U.S. evidence, we find no support for green window dressing among EU-domiciled funds. This study provides the first empirical test of green window dressing in the highly regulated EU ESG climate. The results suggest that stricter ESG regulations and higher levels of ESG maturity in the EU may limit the prevalence of green window dressing.

records.title: Net Payout Yield and Payout Financing: Evidence from the Cross Section of Stock Returns
records.abstract: We replicate that net payout yield (dividends plus share repurchases minus net equity issuance) outperforms dividend yield in the cross-section of stock returns. We demonstrate that the predictive power of net payout yield is conditional on the financing source of payouts. For firms that simultaneously raise net positive debt and make payouts, the net payout yield return relationship is attenuated. This conditional relationship is obscured under ordinary least squares (OLS) due to right-skewness in the return distribution of debt-financing firms but is robustly shown by least absolute deviation (LAD). While point estimate discounts are larger for persistent than for occasional debt-financing firms, we find no statistically significant difference between the two subgroups in the monthly cross-section.

records.title: Repricing Policy Uncertainty: News-Based and Prediction-Market Evidence on U.S. Equity Risk Premia
records.abstract: This paper studies the evolving relationship between economic and political uncertainty, equity prices, and risk premiums. We extend the methodology of Brogaard and Detzel (2015) based on the Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index, enabling the incorporation of a novel entropy-based measure derived from prediction markets. With increased precision, we find that both the contemporaneous and predictive historical relationships between EPU and market returns remain, even as EPU has decoupled from business-cycle variables. Furthermore, our market-based entropy measure appears insufficiently distinct from continuous uncertainty proxies, ultimately failing to generalise as an uncertainty measure or reliably forecast equity returns.

records.title: Convenience Yields in the TIPS-Treasury Bond Mispricing
records.abstract: The TIPS-Treasury bond puzzle, documented by Fleckenstein, Longstaff, and Lustig (2014), describes a persistent and economically significant violation of the no-arbitrage relationship between U.S. nominal Treasury securities, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), and inflation swaps. We empirically test an explanation that has been suggested but not yet studied directly: that the convenience yield of nominal Treasury securities accounts for the mispricing. Following van Binsbergen, Diamond, and Grotteria (2022), we measure the convenience yield as the spread between box rates implied by S&P 500 options and nominal Treasury yields, and we incorporate it into the no-arbitrage relationship. Using daily data from June 2007 to August 2025 at 1-, 2-, and 3-year tenors, we find that adjusting for the convenience yield reduces the average absolute deviation from no-arbitrage conditions by 5 to 10 basis points per annum and eliminates the directional bias previously documented in the literature. The convenience yield does not, however, explain time-series variation in the mispricing outside of the Great Financial Crisis. We interpret these findings as evidence that the convenience yield resolves the puzzle's most distinctive feature - its consistent direction - but acts primarily as a level shifter rather than a driver of high-frequency variation. Our results support including convenience yields alongside TIPS liquidity premia, Treasury credit risk, and intermediation frictions in any complete account of the puzzle.

records.title: Talk, Walk, and the CSRD: Evidence on the Disclosure-Performance Gap
records.abstract: Whether mandatory sustainability disclosure reflects real corporate performance is central to evaluating the effectiveness of recent regulation. This paper studies whether the first year of the EU's Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive narrowed the gap between firms' sustainability disclosure ("talk") and third-party-assessed performance ("walk"). We exploit the directive's 500-employee scope threshold in a difference-in-differences design on 132 European listed firms observed from 2021 to 2024. The composite talk-walk gap widens after CSRD, and the widening is concentrated in the environmental dimension. A decomposition shows that the change reflects a surge in disclosure language with no movement in assessed performance.
